Andy Burnham has hailed a deal between Denmark and the US to "strengthen security in the Arctic" after the two countries resolved a months-long feud over Greenland.
The UK prime minister and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region" in a call on Sunday morning, Downing Street said.
Nato previously said the agreement would help stabilise the region, while Trump declared Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic.
Burnham's comments come as he is expected to meet Trump for the first time at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York this week.
The agreement comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic Arctic location for defence purposes as well as its mineral wealth.
No text of the agreement has been released, but Trump said in a Truth Social post that the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and meant it could "do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland".
He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".
A No 10 spokesperson said in a readout of Sunday's phone call that Burnham and Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region and underlined the strategic and shared importance of the High North for Euro-Atlantic security".
The spokesperson added: "The prime minister congratulated Prime Minister Frederiksen and the Kingdom of Denmark on negotiating a deal benefiting the US, Greenland and Denmark, and said he would pass on his congratulations to President Trump."
While Burnham praised the agreement, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory and a nearly identical to the existing agreement.
"Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said during a Q&A at the Lib Dem party conference.
"So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."
Trump had for months threatened to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.
Following the announcement of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.
The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.
Burnham has spoken to Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intended to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home", including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

Several of the rebel groups which have been fighting the Ethiopian authorities in different parts of the country have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa.
The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival.
The seven groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction, and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration.
Federal authorities have not yet responded.
Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country.
There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions.
An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement.
Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Ogaden, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz â making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states.
Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces during the Tigray war.
It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm.
The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018.
The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea.
Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities".
"Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July.
The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties.
The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results.
The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll.

A former police officer accused of using his work gun to kill a Sydney couple was driven by a "jealous infatuation" with his ex, a court has heard.
Beaumont Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two charges of domestic violence-related murder and one of aggravated break and enter.
Prosecutors allege Lamarre-Condon shot his ex-partner, 26-year-old TV presenter Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies, a 29-year-old Qantas flight attendant, at a home in the Sydney suburb of Paddington in 2024.
The couple's bodies were found in a rural area 200km away, hidden in surfboard bags. The trial is expected to run for three months.
In his opening address on Monday, prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC described how Lamarre-Condon had developed an "obsessive and jealous infatuation" with Baird after a brief romantic relationship.
It manifested itself in a "range of compulsive behaviour", Hatfield said, which escalated when Baird ended all contact in November 2023.
The barrister said Lamarre-Condon used a friend's phone to message Baird and claim he had cancer, stalked his ex-lover, and tampered with his car in the weeks after their break-up.
On the day of the alleged murders, Lamarre-Condon had set his alarm for 04.30 local time, Hatfield claimed, and sent a text to a friend which read: "I'll try to call you tonight and update you... there's no sign I'm doing it".
Lamarre-Condon then switched to a burner phone, picked up a rental car and waited outside Baird's home for three hours dressed as an Uber driver, the prosecution alleged. He had previously bought a surfboard bag to dispose of Baird's body, Hatfield said.
After entering Baird's home with a key he had previously obtained, Lamarre-Condon shot Baird in the kitchen and then killed Davies in the bedroom as he was trying to call emergency services for help, the court was told.
Hatfield said that the accused had planned Baird's murder, and killed Davies so as to "eliminate him as a witness".
In the hours and days after the alleged killings, Lamarre-Condon tried to cover up the murder, Hatfield said, including sending messages from Baird's mobile phone.
The aggravated break and enter charge that Lamarre-Condon is facing refers to an incident in August 2023 where it's alleged he broke into Baird's home and stole his phone and wallet.
Hatfield also told the court that Lamarre-Condon had earlier offered to plead guilty to a single charge of manslaughter relating to Baird's death but this was rejected.
Police were first alerted to the alleged murders after bloodied items belonging to Baird and Davies were found in a bin in Sydney's south.
Later that week, Lamarre-Condon handed himself in to a police station and was charged.
Eight days after the alleged killings took place, authorities found the couple's bodies.
Lamarre-Condon was sacked by New South Wales Police in the weeks after he was charged with the alleged murders.
Before the opening address on Monday, a 15-member jury was selected, with the judge, Justice Natalie Adams, explaining that three extra people were chosen - a jury is typically made up of 12 people - as a contingency for sickness and other unforeseen circumstances.

Three suspects have been detained in South Africa in connection with the murder of a woman in an area east of Johannesburg â the last of nine recent cases in that region that has shone a spotlight on the level of violence against women in the country.
Under pressure to solve the spate of murders which has involved victims' bodies being dumped on a roadside, police have described the arrests of the three â a man and two women - as a "breakthrough".
Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice".
The three suspects are due in court on Monday morning.
Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday.
Several of the recent victims were discovered partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.

The News
House Democrats are fighting over the pecking order in their extended leadership hierarchy as they hope to win the majority.
In recent days, allies of both Reps. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., and Ted Lieu, D-Calif., have laid claim to the fourth-ranking slot in the majority as they look to potentially convert their current titles (assistant Democratic leader and caucus vice chair, respectively), into the equivalent roles in the majority (assistant speaker and caucus chair).
Top Democrats are publicly staying above the fray. âWe have a great team,â said Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., âEverybody has a role to play, and everybodyâs valued.â
A person close to leadership noted that Minority Whip Katherine Clark was considered the fourth-ranking Democrat when she was the assistant speaker under Nancy Pelosi.
A senior political adviser to House Democratic leadership said the âtradition continues as it has been.â
Democratsâ internal rules lay out an election order, though the Houseâs website lists Lieu above Neguse.
âIâm laser-focused on flipping the House. American families are struggling with high costs, and democracy is literally on the line,â Lieu said in a statement.
Know More
Itâs not the first time thereâs been ambiguity in the hierarchy. The last occupant of Neguseâs job, Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., created some murkiness when he stepped down from his top leadership position and into the assistant leader job by taking himself out of the line of leadership succession.
Thereâs not much practical implication of the leadership hierarchy besides dictating the speaking order at press conferences, but it can give lawmakers bragging rights or set them up for future jobs.
Members of the current top trio â House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Clark, and Aguilar â all previously served in the rung of leadership below Pelosiâs top tier, though the order of those roles didnât make a difference for the jobs they hold now.
Additional Democrats are still maneuvering for other jobs in the leadership chain. Lawmakers in the mix for the DCCC chair include Reps. Lizzie Fletcher, D-Texas, Brad Schneider, D-Ill., Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., and Steven Horsford, D-Nev. Two are squaring off for vice chair: Reps. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., and Lauren Underwood, D-Ill.
At least three Democrats are vying to join two open spots on the party messaging arm: Reps. Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., Sarah McBride, D-Del., and Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif.
The top Education and Workforce Committee Democrat, Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, is also facing challenges, with Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-Conn., actively running and Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, D-Ore., weighing a bid.

The Scoop
One month before the Pentagon announced its first equity stake in a company, its top lawyer asked the White House to explain why the deal wouldnât break the law.
The White House budget office responded with a previously unreported legal opinion, reviewed by Semafor, that provides a crucial look at how the Trump administration justified one of its most controversial deployments of taxpayer money in the private sector.
A multibillion-dollar agreement with rare earth firm MP Materials is exempt from the law that bars the executive branch from spending taxpayer money without Congress, Office of Management and Budget General Counsel Mark Paoletta argued in June 2025, because it was ânecessary to avoid an imminent threat to human life and government property.â
The Pentagon would be relying on authorities provided by the Defense Production Act and annual defense legislation from 2017, Paoletta continued, as well as Article II of the Constitution. The deal would be the latest in a âvenerable tradition of presidential obligations in advance of appropriation,â he concluded, stretching back to 1792.
While the Pentagon went on to strike more deals for equity in companies âÂ including its most recent agreement with Venezuelan oil company North American Blue Energy Partners â former Pentagon officials told Semafor they were skeptical of Paolettaâs reasoning. For the moment, the Defense Departmentâs investments are operating in a legal morass that lawmakers in both parties see as unsustainable.
The Senate Armed Services Committee wants Congress to pass its already-advancing plan to give the Pentagonâs Office of Strategic Capital explicit legal authority for its equity stakes, a spokesperson for Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., told Semafor. OSC, which was created to issue loans, has been involved in a majority of the equity agreements.
Wicker âbelieves that an appropriately scoped equity investment authority is important for continued positive work in restoring a free market for critical minerals,â the spokesperson added. âBut he also believes the department must regularize the process surrounding equity-based deals and increase its transparency with the Congress to render this approach sustainable over the long term.â
One former Pentagon official said that the law barring taxpayer expenditures without Congress, known as the Antideficiency Act, was âone of the hurdles we thought was going to be insurmountableâ for the MP Materials deal.
Another former OSC official said they were âsurprised that the current team has discovered the authority to do this under the Defense Production Act,â adding that âlaws can be elastic, but elasticity snaps at some point.â
âI think this pushes the boundaries,â the official continued.
OSCâs role in the MP Materials deal was limited to a $150 million loan under its statute, a Pentagon spokesperson told Semafor, while the Pentagonâs Acquisitions and Sustainment Unit made the $400 million equity investment using authorities granted by the Defense Production Act. Both agreements were authorized by law, the spokesperson said, ading that the latter has already netted more than $465 million.
But those comments are at odds with what a US official told reporters earlier this month in announcing the Venezuela oil deal â that the Trump administration wielded legal authority âgranted to the OSC when it was created.â
The US official added that OSC âhas taken several similar positions in other companies.â Press releases and SEC filings for other deals also seem to blur the line.
The Senate Armed Services panel has requested briefings from the OSC on the Pentagonâs legal authority to take equity, people familiar with the talks said. A spokesperson for the Pentagon said it subsequently responded in depth to questions that arose in the briefing on the MP Materials deal.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the conflicting explanations given for OSCâs role in the Pentagonâs equity deals.
Know More
The Pentagon has negotiated equity or some equivalent, like warrants, in at least 10 companies since Cerberus cofounder Steve Feinberg was confirmed as deputy defense secretary last year. At least seven of those agreements involved the OSC, which is helmed by Cerberus alumnus David Lorch.
Behind the scenes, former Pentagon officials described a rush to strike the deals that raised concerns about due diligence, which were heightened when a deal with rare earths startup Reelement faltered.

The News
President Donald Trumpâs new Canada tariffs are infuriating Democrats and annoying some Republicans â but Congress is unlikely to vote on them before the election.
Trumpâs use of a nearly century-old law to impose the levies takes away individual senatorsâ ability to force such a vote on the Senate floor like they did with the previous set of Canada tariffs, which were imposed under a different statute, noted Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. And that means Republican committee chairmen and leaders control any effort to curtail them â not rank-and-file Democrats.
âThe other tariff statutes donât have this privileged motion that a single senator can force a vote on the floor,â Kaine said.
He added that tariff opponents can write bills to block the tariffs, but under Republicans, âthey get sent to a committeeâ and âthe committee bottles it up.â Instead, Democrats are eyeing pre-election Iran war votes.
Know More
Just last year, individual senators used their powers under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to vote to block earlier Canada tariffs, but thereâs no such option this time around. Itâs no secret that Democrats would like to see Republicans have to take as many tough votes as possible right up until the election, although itâs also possible some GOP incumbents would vote against the tariffs given the option, knowing full well that Trump would veto any effort to undercut his tariff power.
Democrats are still on track to force votes to restrain Trumpâs war powers on Iran, having teed up a resolution written by Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., Kaine said. Those votes are increasingly challenging for some GOP senators as the war drags on.
âWeâre trying to do one every week. Sometimes the schedule makes it hard, but our goal is to do one every week until warâs over,â Kaine said.
Democrats are surprisingly bullish on succeeding with their Iran war votes; theyâd need five Republicans to vote with them if Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., continues to break with his party in order to get enough GOP support to get a simple majority. But there are scheduling battles playing out behind the scenes.
The Senate is still working on the bipartisan college sports bill for the foreseeable future, and Republicans want to hold votes on regulatory rollbacks in exchange for another vote on the Iran war. Thereâs likely to be some horse-trading to get those votes over the next two weeks.

Questions about the USâ relationship with Taiwan will likely take a back seat to trade, AI, and other issues as President Donald Trump welcomes Chinese leader Xi Jinping to Washington.
Still, rising tensions over the self-governing island loom in the background, as the Iran war depletes the USâ weapons stockpile and Taiwanâs AI chip production raises the stakes for any potential conflict.
âI donât think that Taiwan will be as prominent an issue at the summit as it was last May,â the German Marshall Fundâs Bonnie Glaser told Semafor.
She added, however, that Xi will likely âwarn that US arms sales to Taiwan would undermine the leadersâ consensus on having a relationship of constructive strategic stability.â
Reports suggest that Trump plans to delay an already stalled Taiwan arms package until after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November; thatâd leave Taipei and its Washington allies nervous.

The stage is set for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to meet this week, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had a âvery successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AIâ on Sunday.
Officials picked up where they âleft off in Beijing,â Bessent said, and discussed AI and how to âoperationalizeâ the Board of Trade ahead of Xiâs arrival in Washington Wednesday.
They specifically discussed standing up a formal dialogue for the US and China on AI, Bessent said, and made plans to meet again.
He added that the US proposed a US-China ânotification mechanismâ for AI incidents that pose threats to national security, which would include a âshared visionâ of âcommon threats.â
On trade, the countries are weighing which ârelatively small subsetâ of goods could be considered by the Board of Trade rather than through a national security review, Greer said, pointing to consumer goods; âlow-techâ items; energy-related products; agricultural goods; and medical devices.

47ffa8f19ef4.text:
The News
It was a scary weekend in European capitals, where leaders fretted about Russia testing NATOâs limits and grappled with a threatened drawdown of American troops in Europe.
French President Emanuel Macron delivered a briefing to the candidates running to succeed him so disturbing that even the far-right National Rallyâs leaders emerged denouncing Russian hybrid attacks.
The looming question is whether European leaders, institutions, and citizens can pivot swiftly enough so that the bloc can use its economic heft to take responsibility for its own security. One institution is testing that: Sciences Po, the training ground for French and other European policy elites, has sharply redirected its resources to the moment. This fall, it launched a new Centre for Global Security and Governance and expanded its defense and intelligence offerings, the schoolâs president, Luis Vassy, told Semafor.
âWe had been the school of happy globalization,â he said in a phone interview from Paris on Sunday. âWe need to readjust the mindset of future European elites to a world that is going to be more competitive, more brutal.â
âThat doesnât mean we should dissolve our value system, but if we believe itâs a value system that is worth defending, that has some consequences in terms of the way we should act,â he said.
Sciences Po, which also recently launched a climate school to meet the other looming crisis, had long lacked the sort of security-minded focus on âinternational relationsâ present at big American universities â take, for example, Johns Hopkins SAIS and Columbia University SIPA.
The field âin its US shape is seen as a right-wing domain, because it is states, itâs power, itâs conflict,â Vassy said. âIf you look at issues more from the bottom-up, you look more into social trends, the oppressive nature of the state, et cetera.â
But his students have already begun to pivot for the new moment: Defense and security majors in the existing policy school have increased 30% per year for the last three years, he said, and the school of international affairs is launching new concentrations in defense and intelligence to meet the rising demand. This reflects a new consensus that, however far Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth take their current campaign, a new era has begun.
âIf India can be independent from a defense standpoint thereâs no reason Europeans shouldnât,â said Vassy, a former French diplomat in Washington and chief of staff to the Foreign Ministry. âItâs simply not reasonable to have your whole security depending on a foreign actor.â
Sciences Poâs graduates typically supply about three-quarters of the enrollees at the training academy for French leaders known as ENA. Barring a cultural revolution, its current students will more or less be running the country from about 2045 to 2070.
Benâs view
Even as European leaders press forward to centralize the blocâs economy and invest in its shared security, the rising politics in Germany and France are pulling those nations in the opposite direction. The radical AfD in Germany and moderating National Rally in France are both focused on ending immigration and enjoy support from voters wary of escalating conflict with Russia.
The longer-term trend, though, is clear. Sciences Poâs turn reflects a European assumption that, whatever happens in the US elections in 2026 and 2028, the American security umbrella is receding over the long term.
âI worked in the foreign ministry where we could happily lecture the rest of the world. This is completely outside their worldview,â said Vassy. Instead, the new classes are âextremely conscious about the challenges. They have not been educated like you and me in a world where the West was the unique center of power.â
Room for Disagreement
âThe European Union is a vehicle for economic cooperation. It is a peace project, not a war project,â Hugo Bromley wrote in Foreign Affairs in March, arguing that an attempt to build a common European defense front would turn into a domestic political disaster.
Notable
- Vassy laid out his views recently in Grand Continent: âWe have moved from a world where we projected ourselves with our ideas, our values, and our strengths, to a world that projects itself onto us,â he wrote, according to a translation from French.

The Scene
MOKOPANE, South Africa â In South Africaâs northernmost province, under a cavernous expanse of jagged gray rock, lies a mineral treasure trove that could play a pivotal role in the countryâs relationship with global superpowers.
It is from here that South Africa has sought to rebuild a humiliating relationship with Donald Trumpâs Washington and bolster a budding one with Beijing, pitching itself as a critical minerals supplier to the rival powers. According to South African government documents and market data reviewed by Semafor, as well as interviews with senior officials and executives, Pretoria is seeking to leverage its role as the worldâs dominant supplier of platinum to ingratiate itself with Washington and Beijing at the same time.
The US and China are both seeking to secure access to platinum group metals â prized for withstanding extreme heat, conducting electricity, and resisting corrosion. The US needs platinum for catalytic converters, as it looks to grow its automotive industry based on internal-combustion engines and hybrids, and defense equipment; Beijing to develop green hydrogen as a form of sustainable energy. And both need the metals to build the data centers that will power their AI buildouts.
Yet the superpowers have taken sharply different approaches to trade policy with Pretoria. Washington slapped a 30% import duty on South African goods last year as part of a wider strategy of trade pressure: Since returning to office last year, US President Donald Trump has accused Pretoria of presiding over a âwhite genocideâ â a discredited claim he repeated during a fractious Oval Office meeting with his South African counterpart. His administration has also demanded the rollback of land expropriation policies and Black Economic Empowerment laws, which were established to redress the legacy of apartheid. Tensions over these issues, exacerbated by Pretoriaâs criticism of Israel over its conduct in Gaza, have become a major sticking point.
That has helped push Africaâs largest economy closer to China. South Africa hosted China and Iran in Beijing-led naval drills this year, a public show of devotion to the BRICS bloc that further fueled Washingtonâs ire. Beijing, for its part, scrapped levies on South African imports entirely as part of its move this year to extend its zero-tariff policy across the continent.
At the core of South Africaâs push to reset its ties with the US while maintaining strong relations with China are mines like the giant Mogalakwena site, 150 miles north of Johannesburg and operated by Valterra Platinum. The worldâs largest open-pit mine, dotted with yellow tipper trucks carving out boulders and overlooked by the rose-tinged peaks of Limpopo provinceâs Waterberg mountains, sits on top of the Bushveld Igneous Complex, a mineral deposit formed around two billion years ago which is now roughly the size of Sri Lanka. The deposit is a geological anomaly, home to around 80% of the worldâs known PGM reserves.
âIf you check all over the world,â Sello Mashabela, a Valterra geologist said as he gazed at the huge pit, âyou wonât really find anything like this.â
Know More
Pretoria has pushed its dominant position in the PGM space â the second-largest reserves of the metals are found in Russia, and therefore functionally off-limits to Western firms because of sanctions over the Ukraine war â to the core of its trade policy.
In a document published in May and reviewed by Semafor, full details of which have not been previously reported, South Africaâs trade ministry emphasized the importance of PGMs to US industry when making the case for the African Growth and Opportunity Act, a trade agreement, to be extended by 15 years.
âSouth Africa supplies the United States with 12 of the 50 minerals identified by the United States Geological Survey as critical for United States interests,â the ministry wrote in a submission to the Office of the US Trade Representative, arguing that materials such as PGM metals âare important to United States production and technological advancement, and South Africa has maintained reliable supply.â It urged the US to pursue an âinvestment-led trade strategyâ that included local processing in Africa. In a separate document dated May 15, 2026, also seeking an AGOA extension, Business Unity South Africa, the countryâs largest trade body, stressed PGMs were âessential to US manufacturing, defence, technology, and the energy transition.â
That push fell short: US lawmakers this month voted to extend the AGOA pact, but by just two years. Yet officials are not giving up. South Africaâs ministry of trade, industry, and competition told Semafor that critical minerals were a central part of the countryâs trade negotiations with Washington. Kaamil Alli, spokesman for the countryâs trade minister, said South African officials were holding discussions with US companies interested in securing critical mineral supplies.
Pretoria wants American investors to build smelters, factories, and processing facilities in South Africa, rather than relying principally on conventional offtake agreements with local mines. âWe understand you want these minerals for particular reasons, but this is our goal,â Alli said, describing Pretoriaâs pitch. âCome and letâs have a mutually beneficial relationship where you undertake processing in South Africa.â
Alli said talks on this issue were expected to continue in New York during the United Nations General Assembly this week. Senior South African trade officials plan to meet US business representatives, while Trade Minister Parks Tau is also likely to hold talks with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

Paul Nestadt is about as steeped in suicide prevention as a person can be.
He treats suicidal patients as a psychiatrist, has co-authored scores of research papers on how and why people kill themselves, and teaches graduate courses on the subject.
But he’ll be the first to admit: “I can’t tell you which of my patients is likely to die by suicide in the next six months.”
Almost nobody can.
Research shows predictions of who will be suicidal are only slightly better than a coin toss. And they haven’t improved over 50 years.
But that doesn’t make Nestadt hopeless. Instead, it pushes him to pursue interventions that don’t require pinpointing people at risk.
Chief among them: making it harder for people to carry out the act of killing themselves.
“Instead of asking every doctor to figure out which patient will die by suicide and locking that patient up, it might be that we need to make sure there aren’t loaded guns available,” Nestadt said.
In an ongoing series, KFF Health News is examining approaches to suicide prevention that expand beyond providing people at risk with medication and therapy. Although those are lifesaving measures, many clinicians, researchers, and people who have lost loved ones to suicide agree that more is needed. The challenge is that when it comes to firearms, broad policy approaches quickly become constitutionally complicated and politically polarizing.
Research shows that limiting access to lethal means is one of the most promising approaches to save lives. It can involve erecting barriers on buildings and bridges to prevent people from jumping, as well as decreasing the number of pills someone can buy or be prescribed at once.
“That’s the one that will save the most lives,” said Nestadt, medical director at the Johns Hopkins Center for Suicide Prevention.
It may also be the most difficult to achieve.
More than 28,000 people killed themselves with a gun last year, representing more than half of all suicide deaths in the U.S., according to preliminary federal data. Even as overall suicide rates have dipped recently, gun suicides have hit record highs for five years in a row.
Many of the deaths are among middle-aged white men and veterans, two groups that have had high suicide rates for years. But more recently, gun suicides have risen among women and among some Black and Latino men. Researchers say a surge in first-time gun buyers during the covid pandemic underscores the need for prevention efforts that can be applied widely.
Some people assume it’s futile to restrict access to bridges, pills, or guns. The thinking goes: Those who want to kill themselves will simply find another way.
But research refutes that. Creating barriers for one method doesn’t typically push people to another.
Suicide risk can surge quickly, with people spending less than an hour or even five minutes between deciding to die and acting on it. Anything that delays such action — for example, having to unlock a safe to access a gun — gives them time to reconsider or for someone to intervene.
However, in the U.S., discussion around guns — even in the context of a traditionally bipartisan topic such as suicide prevention — is a political lightning rod. Mentions of background checks, waiting periods, or red flag laws often send people running to their respective corners. Gun owners and the firearm industry say many of the policies suicide prevention advocates seek threaten their Second Amendment rights, and many policymakers see the topic as a nonstarter.
President Donald Trump has been a strong ally of gun owners. His administration has rolled back dozens of firearms regulations and rescinded a previous surgeon general’s warning that called gun violence a public health crisis. It has also revoked grants focused on addressing community gun violence and cut federal staff working on the issue.
The White House did not respond to specific questions about how these actions may affect the nation’s high rate of gun suicides or what it’s doing to prevent such deaths. But spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that “President Trump is committed to Making America Healthy Again and that includes mental health.” She pointed to the administration’s support for developing psychedelic treatments for mental illness and an announcement of $52.5 million in grants for veteran suicide prevention.
The Limits of Red Flag Laws
One gun policy that has gained some traction, despite pushback, is the extreme risk protection order, more commonly known as a red flag law.
Adopted in some form in 22 states and the District of Columbia, these laws allow judges to temporarily remove a person’s guns when evidence suggests they pose a danger to themself or others.
Although such laws are often passed in the wake of mass shootings, research suggests they’re more effective at preventing suicide.
Still, they require identifying someone at risk.
Someone like Dorothy Paugh’s dad.
In 1965, when Paugh was a young girl, her dad lost his job. He was distressed, not knowing how he’d support his wife and five children, Paugh said. He reviewed his life insurance policy, told his wife where he kept important documents, and bought a handgun.
“If my mom had been able to get an extreme risk protection order or if Dad’s best friend had asked to hold his gun for a while, maybe my dad would not have shot himself. He might have lived,” Paugh said.
Decades later, Paugh advocated for a red flag law in Maryland and sat in the legislative gallery when the measure was passed.
She believes the law is saving lives.
Studies across other states show that for every 10 to 20 guns removed under red flag laws, one suicide is averted, saving a life.
But Paugh also recognizes the law’s limitations.
“It wouldn’t have saved my son,” she said.

There is now a three-week international break with no Premier League games until 10 October.
We are five matches into the league season and there is a long way to go in the campaign, but which teams have impressed so far and who have disappointed?
You can have your say in the comments at the bottom of the page.
Arsenal: Solid start to their title defence until they were ripped apart by Brighton having survived a penalty scare at Sunderland. 7
Aston Villa: Signs they are beginning to move in the right direction after losing so many key players during the transfer window. 6
Bournemouth: If games lasted 80 minutes the Cherries would be near the top of the table. Need to cut out conceding so late. 6
Brentford: Demolished Spurs and Chelsea without fuss during a highly impressive unbeaten start. Can they keep it up and challenge for Europe? 8
Brighton: Kings of entertainment after hitting 16 goals in five top-flight games, including three against champions Arsenal. A joy to watch. 9
Chelsea: After a strong start under Xabi Alonso, the Blues have lost two of their past three - and were picked apart by Brentford. Are they really moving in the right direction? 6
Coventry City: You could hear the sighs of relief in the away end at Nottingham Forest on Saturday. Will Frank Lampard's side kick on after that win? 6
Crystal Palace: Room for improvement after one win and three defeats. 5
Everton: Despite a transfer window to forget, David Moyes has made the Toffees hard to beat. 6
Fulham: Decent draws against Liverpool and Manchester United but need a win. Ipswich (away) followed by Hull (home), Coventry (away) and Crystal Palace (home) offer hope when they return from the international break. 5
Hull City: To have eight points from a tough opening five fixtures is an excellent return, including beating Manchester United and drawing with Aston Villa and Chelsea. 8
Ipswich Town: Defensively vulnerable but two late winners, against Sunderland and Crystal Palace, have earned them six points and shown their fighting spirit. 5
Leeds United: Fifth in the league, unbeaten and with the joint-best defensive record. They showed what they are capable of with a superb 4-1 win over Newcastle. 7
Liverpool: Unbeaten but have been far from their best. Three clean sheets in their past three games, but more is expected from Andoni Iraola's side. 6
Manchester City: Five league games, five victories. Managed to win at Manchester United despite going down to 10 men midway through the first half. With Erling Haaland already top scorer, City fans will expect a real push to win the league. 9
Manchester United: Disappointing performances to lose at Hull and draw at a Fulham side who were bottom of the league. Their only win so far came against Ipswich and they were denied a victory at Everton by a late equaliser. 4
Newcastle United: A mixed bag under new manager Matthias Jaissle. They impressed in a draw against Liverpool, won comfortably at Tottenham, but were also terrible in a loss at Leeds, although they responded well to beat Hull. 6
Nottingham Forest: Their best results have come away, drawing at Liverpool and winning at Aston Villa. But their home form will be a huge worry - yet to score a goal and with only one point from three matches at the City Ground. 5
Sunderland: After coming seventh in 2025-26, Sunderland fans will have wanted a better start to this season. The Black Cats gave good accounts of themselves against Arsenal and Manchester City, but lost both matches. 5
Tottenham Hotspur: After spending more than Â£300m in the summer, Spurs have been poor, failing to score in their opening four league matches. Supporters will be demanding an instant improvement after the international break. 2

The Scene
With drones and missiles still being regularly intercepted overhead, BlueFive Capital founder and CEO Hazem Ben-Gacem cooked up a play in the defense industry, over a Ramadan meal with companions with ties to a Gulf sovereign fund.
Six months later, BlueFive is âready to launch it,â Ben-Gacem told Semafor in an interview in Dubai, while staying coy on further details. At the helm of one of the regionâs fastest-growing funds, Abu Dhabi-based BlueFive Capital is not slowing down, even in wartime, and Ben-Gacem says neither are the Gulfâs sovereigns; he counts members of each of the regionâs royal families, except Qatar, as founding shareholders.
The 30-year veteran of Investcorp left in 2024 to found BlueFive, which now has $15 billion in assets under management. Among its deals in the last year, it has taken a 30% stake in supercar company Bugatti and backed an Islamic digital bank.
While Ben-Gacem said fundraising isnât easy â âitâs a pain in the you-know-what,â he said to a group of private capital investors in Dubai last week â BlueFiveâs $3 billion Onyx Fund, to back AI, biotech, and advanced computing in the US and Europe, was closed just before the war. Pitchbook called it a âstandoutâ in an otherwise muted year for regional private equity.
The firmâs AI strategy reflects, in part, demographics in the Gulf, which relies on expat labor, especially for its services and tourism industries. âAddressing [that gap] today through automation is an important trend,â he said. âNot much different from what Thailand and China are doing.â BlueFive has opened an office in Beijing and will add another in Indonesia, the worldâs most-populous Muslim nation, to seize on growing demand for Islamic products.
âThe same way I feel good having a âMade in Italyâ label on my suit, when Iâm in Jakarta or Kuala Lumpur, and I buy a Sharia-compliant product I want to have a âMade in Meccaâ label on it,â he said.
Ben-Gacem is eyeing another, more unusual target: BlueFive could look to do a deal for one of the regionâs local stock exchanges, to convert to an exchange for digital assets.
Q&A
Kelsey Warner: We find ourselves sitting in a regional war and facing a lot of uncertainty. What have been the challenges for you this year?
Hazem Ben-Gacem: This is not like World War Z where people are running around and scared and supermarkets are empty. Iâm surprised that thereâs no difference in the pace and scale of investment, particularly in those strategic sectors that continue to accelerate: technology, agri [and food security], infra.
The bulk of our LPs tend to be entrepreneurial sovereign pockets. Our discussions are not, âletâs slow down.â Itâs more like âwe want to do this, can you do it with us?â Even the smaller ones, even Bahrain, have a clear agenda where they want to deploy their capital. Obviously, a lot of it is strategic maneuvering to make sure they are prepared for the future, and thatâs what our conversations tend to be about, as opposed to more defensive lines.
Youâve opened an office in Beijing and invested in a Chinese AI generative video company. Whatâs the strategy there?
We have set up quite a substantial team out of Beijing. We deployed about $1.2 billion in China. A lot of those investments are for the purpose of technology transfer to the [Gulf region]. We announced the first such business called CargoX, which is autonomous delivery.
We should be announcing a presence in Jakarta, the worldâs most populous Muslim nation. Iâm really surprised by this increased appetite for Islamic products. I didnât expect it. I felt like the world has moved away from that, and thatâs getting the biggest traction in Southeast Asia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Bangladesh, India. We took over one of the big Sharia-compliant asset managers, Sidra Capital. Now, why is that? The same way I feel good having a âMade in Italyâ label on my suit, when Iâm in Jakarta or Kuala Lumpur, and I buy a Sharia-compliant product I want to have a âMade in Meccaâ label on it. Thatâs priceless.
If you had to give advice to your peers in the region about striking out on their own, what would you tell them?
The region is tribal still. Our investors, itâs not like they havenât seen Blackstone or Goldman Sachs or Accel Partners or Andreessen Horowitz. But they give us money. Because itâs much more than just, Iâm an LP and Iâm going to give money to this GP to make my returns. I want to do it with a partner I trust.
Notable
- BlueFive Capital is in the mix for a possible take-private of US fast-food chain Wendyâs as Nelson Peltzâs Trian Fund Management works on a deal with backing from a consortium of investors, the Financial Times reported.

Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees who have fled to Djibouti
Fighting on Yemen's west coast has prompted thousands of people to flee by boat across the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti over the last ten days.
The BBC's Frank Gardner visited a refugee camp in Obock, a small port town where officials are preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees.
The UN International Organisation for Migration said people were âtravelling on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water.
The crossings were sparked by an offensive by the Iran-backed Houthi movement to take control of a key island and seize the strategically important port of Mokha.

- Published
CNN, Politico and MS NOW have said they will sue the Trump administration after the three US media outlets were barred from the White House.
President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the three organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his government.
The companies said their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized when attempting to access the building on Saturday.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes".
The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
"Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," the CNN, Politico and MS NOW statement continued.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
BBC News has asked the White House for comment.
Announcing the ban last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".
The US president added that there "may be others to join them".
When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."
He has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.
Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

The Scoop
The data center buildout is driving a rush of venture capital investment in clean tech, breathing new life into startups that were at risk of being steamrolled by the Trump administrationâs pullback on climate policy.
Global climate tech venture investment hit $26 billion in the first half of this year, 55% above the previous year, according to climate tech finance tracker Currence.ai. Data centers and the products and services that help them operate are in particularly high demand, with startups in the sector seeing their fundraising and valuations jump. Itâs an opportunity to push some new carbon-cutting tech across the âvalley of deathâ between pilot and commercial scale, to the benefit of the global energy transition at large â but also links clean techâs fortunes to a digital infrastructure buildout whose ultimate scale remains uncertain.
âVenture capital sees the data center opportunity, and is focused on it,â Frank OâSullivan, managing director for energy at VC firm S2G Investments, told Semafor. âThereâs an opportunity over the next little while to see a lot more clean tech success stories emerge. The risk is that the driver of all of this â the data center bubble â might pop.â
Timâs view
This week, climate tech investors will descend en masse on New York for Climate Week, a forum for a vast range of cutting-edge firms to show off and find money. As political support for decarbonizing the existing energy system has dried up, data centers have emerged as a new center of financial gravity, drawing in unprecedented billions from the biggest tech and Wall Street firms. Much, perhaps most, of that investment is going into conventional energy assets that are not necessarily climate-friendly. But with AI companies under intense pressure to reduce their resource consumption â for reasons of cost, if nothing else â a lot is trickling down to tech originally conceived for the energy transition.
âWeâre experiencing a very hot time for a bunch of the stuff we were already in,â said Tom Chi, founding partner of clean tech investor At One Ventures, which focuses on deep tech innovations with environmental benefits. Thatâs setting up potential new windfalls for shops like his: One company in Chiâs portfolio, Blue Energy, a startup building low-cost modular components for advanced nuclear plants aimed at drastically cutting the amount of time needed to build them for data centers, has seen its pre-IPO valuation shoot up by orders of magnitude. That type of growth acts like a beacon to other non-energy investors, and suddenly Chi has found his companiesâ funding rounds increasingly crowded.
âItâs a really weird moment because weâre having a bunch of tourists come in,â he said. âWeâre investing alongside firms that have spent their entire history doing enterprise SaaS, and now theyâre sitting here trying to understand desiccants for cooling systems.â
Conversely, the focus on AI-relevant technologies is pushing climate tech VCs to look in unusual directions: S2G recently invested in Alliance North America, which makes high-end, low-emissions diesel generators. A technology that facilitates fossil fuel consumption âdoesnât seem like it would be in our bailiwick,â OâSullivan said. But because of its use for powering data centers more efficiently, âthat has mushroomed into an enormous opportunity, and suddenly youâre decarbonizing by stealthâ relative to conventional generators.
Room for Disagreement
More capital is usually welcome, Chi said. But firms with less experience, and less in-house engineering expertise, can have unrealistic expectations about the time, capital, and skill required to bring a novel hard tech to scale and profitability compared to software â which could ultimately lead to disappointment and cutbacks. Itâs also likely that as the space becomes more crowded, more mistakes will be made, inflating the valuations of companies that donât really have a strong business model when you get down to the nuts and bolts, and creating conditions for spectacular failures.
And if clean tech startups are only valuable when they have data centers as primary customers, some technologies that are important for emissions reduction will fall through the cracks: VC investment in carbon management tech and low-carbon fuels both plummeted this year, according to Currence.ai.

Florida’s coastal residents know to brace for storm surge, but during 2024’s Hurricane Milton, it was inland communities that suffered some of the greatest flooding.
It took three weeks for water to recede from some neighborhoods, remembered Polk County Commissioner Becky Troutman. Her community, along Central Florida’s busy I-4 corridor, is among the nation’s fastest-growing places. With homes costing an average of $100,000 less than those in Orlando and Tampa, Polk—once known for citrus—is now coveted for its housing stock.
So as the county began to update its comprehensive plan, which governs growth management, leaders had much to consider. Among the questions: After witnessing how bad flooding can be, should they require bigger stormwater ponds in new developments?
But Polk County can’t enact a change like that or, potentially, write new rules to manage the region’s surging growth. That’s because of SB 180, a law the state Legislature adopted last year.
It was presented as a hurricane recovery measure—a way to keep strict measures from foiling rebuilding—but its sweeping language went much further. The law prohibits regulations that are more “burdensome or restrictive” than what’s currently on the books. In Polk, that could include stormwater management rules or more tightly regulated development.
The law, retroactive to Oct. 1, 2024, is supposed to sunset in 2027 unless another natural disaster hits, in which case it resets, freezing development changes for a new recovery period.
SB 180 is a preemption, a law enacted by a higher governmental power to override a lower one’s existing ordinances or prevent new ones. In Florida, legislators are passing these laws with increased frequency, alarming some local officials and government watchdogs. They don’t want localities to lose their authority to protect constituents from matters ranging from urban sprawl to public health, environmental justice and climate change.
“I see it as a freedom issue,” said Raymer Maguire, director of campaigns and policy at the CLEO (Climate Leadership Engagement Opportunities) Institute, a Miami-based organization focused on climate education and advocacy. “Every year, Florida is getting a little less free.”
SB 180 is Florida’s most expansive preemption law, but it is far from the only one. In the past decade, state lawmakers have passed a spate of prohibitions limiting local control over issues such as firearms, LGBTQ issues and, increasingly, environment and climate regulation.
Local communities can no longer require heat breaks for workers. Nor can they ban plastic bags or single-use plastics, mandate the inclusion of EV charging stations in new parking lots or outlaw gas-powered lawn equipment.
They cannot augment environmental protections through “rights of nature” ordinances. And as of this year, cities and counties can’t move toward 100 percent carbon neutrality for the sake of mitigating greenhouse gases or use public funds to incentivize private companies to do so, either.
A bill to amend SB 180, which would have narrowed its scope and reach, failed to pass during this year’s session. The bill’s defeat added to growing bipartisan unease.
“What are we doing if we’re not protecting the very basic functions of local government?” asked Tallahassee City Commissioner Jacqueline “Jack” Porter, a Democrat. “I don’t know why I’m there anymore sometimes except to fight back because our powers are just being slowly eroded more and more every year.”
If the trend continues, “Local officials, maybe, start to become more of a puppet or a placeholder than a decision-maker,” said Troutman, who is part of the all-Republican County Commission in a county that traditionally votes red.
Amplifying Troutman’s concerns is a proposal to slash property taxes, making communities even more dependent on the state and its funding priorities. In Polk County, loss of tax revenue also could derail a land acquisition program voters approved in 2022, when they agreed to increase their millage rate to preserve open space, Troutman said.
A National Trend
Florida is hardly the only state passing more preemptive legislation. The Local Solutions Support Center, a national nonprofit combating “abusive” preemption and advocating for local democracy, is tracking 900 such legislative proposals across the United States.
“If you care about people, if you care about our planet, and if you care about democracy, there is a preemption issue you should be worried about,” said Katie Belanger, the organization’s lead consultant.
Preemption itself is neutral, she explained. What worries her are preemption laws that target certain populations, such as Florida’s prohibition on county- or city-mandated heat breaks. That law, she said, disproportionately hurts a workforce composed largely of lower-income, minority workers.
In pushing for tighter state control, some state lawmakers say Florida’s size, complexity and growth—23.5 million people and a $1.8 trillion economy, the world’s 14th-largest—warrants greater regulatory uniformity. Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has expressed a desire to shred the “patchwork” of policies impacting regional and statewide businesses.
But that’s a tough pivot for Florida’s 67 counties and 411 incorporated municipalities, which have been living under a “home rule” style of governance since it was codified in the state constitution in 1968.
“Quincy, Florida, is going to have the same growth and development rules and regulations as Miami-Dade?” wondered Troutman, comparing the North Florida city with fewer than 10,000 residents to the South Florida metropolis, home to 2.8 million.
“The thing that worries me most is what I refer to as the homogenization of Florida,” said Dana Souza, the Sanibel city manager. His city of roughly 6,000 year-round residents is among the state’s most tightly regulated—by residents’ choice.

Protesters gathered in Austin on Sunday after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and wounded a man in the Texas capital.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan DoorDash delivery driver, was shot in the torso and taken to hospital, his lawyer told US media.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement to the BBC that it was investigating the shooting of a man in Austin who had entered the country illegally.
It is unclear what led to the shooting, and the local mayor and police have demanded an independent probe. It comes months after a man in Houston was shot dead by an ICE officer.
Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told CBS that Garces Perez called his wife while "yelling in pain" in hospital. She told National Public Radio he was in ICE custody.
The Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement efforts and arrests during Trump's second term, sparking unrest across several US cities.
The administration has defended its policies and the agency's controversial tactics as necessary for public safety and to enact Trump's campaign promise to secure the border and carry out mass deportations.
The shooting in Austin on Sunday occurred just before 1300 local time, although details remain scarce.
Dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave Austin.
Local television outlets showed the demonstrators gathering across the street from âa blue Toyota Corolla that â sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby, Reuters news agency reported.
Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said that Austinites have a right to know what happened and "a right to feel safe in their city" during a media briefing on Sunday.
"They should know the truth," he said, adding that he is pleased that the city will also be involved in the investigation.
He added that ICE operations have surged in Austin in recent weeks.
ICE has faced intense scrutiny after a number of deadly shootings, including the death of Houston resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo.
Salgado Araujo had not been a target of an ICE investigation, but was shot during an ICE traffic stop, according to DHS.
Texas Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat, has demanded a full and immediate independent investigation into the latest shooting and the release of body camera footage. He also demanded "accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law".
Activists say that the administration has violated due process as it carries out the crackdown.
Democrats have demanded reforms at the agency, including requiring immigration enforcement agents to wear body cameras and not conceal their faces.
Earlier this month the US Department of Justice charged an ICE agent with lying about the non-fatal shooting of a Venezuelan migrant in Minnesota - a rare instance in which the current justice department accused a federal agent of breaking the law on the job.
Earlier this week, Florida lawmaker Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican who has spoken out against the immigration crackdown, released an advert criticising the targeting and detaining of individuals who have no criminal record.
Salazar appeared on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday and said that she has since spoken to the president, and believes he will keep the country on the right track.
"He gets it more than anybody," she said.

A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes against humanity.
The report by Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said since September last year there had been at least 68 US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific, outside US territorial waters, which killed more than 220 people.
Saul said that even if targets could be identified as members of designated terrorist groups, they had not staged an armed attack on the US which would trigger a right to self-defence under international law.
The report comes two days after the US military said it killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean.
"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southcom, which commands US forces in the region, said in a statement about the latest attack, which was accompanied by a grainy video.
But in a briefing note released by the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Saul said that "such attacks amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law".
"There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law," Saul concluded.
BBC News has contacted the White House and State Department for a response to the report.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously said the overall operation is aimed at removing "narco-terrorists from our hemisphere" and securing the US from "the drugs that are killing our people".
The US military launched the operation, known as "Southern Spear", in early September.
However, officials have not offered definitive evidence that the vessels targeted are involved in trafficking.
Since the beginning, experts have questioned the legality of the strikes, which initially drew strong criticism from Latin American leaders whose citizens have been targeted.
However, NicolÃ¡s Maduro, who was the Venezuelan leader at the time and opposed the strikes, was seized by US forces in a dramatic and highly controversial night-time raid on the capital Caracas at the beginning of this year.
Another outspoken critic of Operation Southern Spear, Colombia's left-wing president at the time, Gustavo Petro, stood down in August after a Trump-backed candidate won June's presidential election.

The annual high-level gathering at the U.N. General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them? READ MORE: Iran-backed Houthi rebels warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's growing civil war And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth? Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The future of the United Nations will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century's major global players. The U.N.'s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful U.N. Security Council, where the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented. Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' second five-year term ends Dec. 31 and no clear successor has emerged. This meeting is still pivotal There is still no question that the U.N. remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting Tuesday along with dozens of ministers. Among the headliners will be U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak Tuesday after Guterres' opening "state of the world" address. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday. READ MORE: Four U.N. secretary-general candidates audition this week. That's far fewer than in 2016 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — whom New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority — will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won't be coming to the U.N. because the U.S. has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day. The United States, under its agreement with the U.N. to host the organization, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings. Equally telling is who else isn't coming. China's President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping — some diplomats say snubbing — the U.N. gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn't coming either, and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out. France's U.N. ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said it is "extremely critical" for world leaders this week to support the U.N. as the place where the world's nations meet — especially at a time of such polarization. "We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation." United Nations has not had a great year There is no doubt it's been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The U.S. failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organization's finances in rocky shape. But veteran U.N. watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group's global issues and institutions program director, says 2025 was even worse. A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his U.N. speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organization. Trump didn't announce a pullout last September and the U.N. muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid. In recent days, the U.S. paid $725 million of its dues to the U.N.'s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly. The payment was a strong indication Trump will keep the U.S. in the United Nations. The U.N. is no longer "in freefall," Gowan said, but it "is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis." Put more graphically, he said, "The U.N. may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future." Former U.N. deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said, "While the world still trusts the U.N., the global public is eager for change." The Strait of Hormuz âcannot be obsolete,â despite the Trump administrationâs assertions, Qatarâs energy minister said. Rejecting US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessentâs view that it could become a âworthless piece of waterâ as alternatives emerge, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi noted the route carries far more than oil and that other goods canât be moved as efficiently by land or air.
Doha has studied exporting gas via pipeline, but decided against it âbased on commercial and technical criteria,â he said at the Qatar Economic Forum. The country plans to expand LNG capacity from 77 million tons per year to 142 million by 2030, and duplicating that infrastructure isnât feasible.
The expansion could be delayed if equipment canât reach Qatar through Hormuz, Al-Kaabi said. The first new LNG plant is expected to start operations next year, and facilities damaged in Iranian strikes will take around three years to repair, he added.

Doha is moving the Qatar Investment Authorityâs domestic assets into a separate unit as it seeks to attract more foreign capital and increase private sector involvement in the economy. bb9216a526a9.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/cnn-ms-now-politico-say-theyve-notified-trump-theyre-suing-over-denied-white-house-access Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter CNN, MS NOW, Politico say they've notified Trump they're suing over denied White House access Politics Sep 21, 2026 7:39 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — CNN, MS NOW and Politico said Monday they've notified President Donald Trump's administration that they're filing a lawsuit over being denied White House access. The three outlets made the announcement in a joint statement posted on X, two days after their reporters were blocked from the White House and prevented from doing their jobs. The reporters' entry badges were disabled on Saturday, a day after Trump had suddenly announced he was barring the outlets because of reporting he found to be "fake news." The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment early Monday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The actions were a clear escalation of Trump's long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and were the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States. White House reporters from the two cable networks — Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW — went live to report they'd been turned away, their press badges deactivated, when arriving for their jobs at the White House. Soon after, Politico said its White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry and had her badge confiscated. "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the outlets said in a joint statement posted early Monday on X. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." In his second term, Trump and his Republican administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action. Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — insulting them in briefings or in his recent speech at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner. The WHCA's president, Jacqui Heinrich, called on the Trump administration to immediately restore the three outlets' access. "The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," Heinrich said. "The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press

Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is under investigation by Swiss prosecutors over allegations he obtained a forged Covid-19 vaccination certificate.
The 33-year-old is alleged to have obtained the certificate in 2022, when it was a requirement in Switzerland for some travel abroad.
The public prosecutor's office of the city of Lucerne confirmed the investigation was under way to determine whether any criminal behaviour took place in obtaining a "false or forged" certificate.
The Sunderland midfielder, who was playing for Arsenal at the time, posted a statement on social media on Monday saying he had a "mistrust" towards the vaccine and had been "influenced by worries and uncertainty".
He said: "In this troubled state of mind I acquired a vaccine certificate, instead of clarifying my unanswered questions in the proper way.
"Today I see clearly, that this way was not correct. It was a mistake. I'm sorry.
"I take responsibility for this decision, will engage with the process of establishing the facts and fully co-operate with the relevant authorities."
The Swiss office of public health confirmed that while there was never a general legal requirement to obtain or hold such a certificate, it was needed for access to various activities, venues and travel, meaning that participation was restricted for anyone who did not possess one.
These measures in Switzerland were in place until spring 2022. After that point, Covid-19 certificates continued to be issued, primarily to enable members of the public to meet entry requirements when travelling abroad.
The Swiss Football Association said Xhaka, the country's record appearance holder with 152 caps, had withdrawn from the Swiss camp for their upcoming Nations League matches against Scotland, North Macedonia and Slovenia following his statement.
It added the decision to withdraw had been made jointly by the player and management and that they would discuss Xhaka's future with the team after the international window.
Switzerland have away fixtures against North Macedonia and Scotland on 26 and 29 September, before facing Slovenia and North Macedonia at home in early October.
Sunderland boss Regis le Bris refused to comment on the allegations following the Black Cats' defeat at Manchester City on Sunday.
"It is not my area to speak about those problems or situations," he said. "My area is football. About football, he is really good."
Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year, where they were knocked out in the quarter-finals by eventual runners-up Argentina.
