German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he will keep his ruling coalition together for the sake of his country's "democratic future", following resounding defeats for his party in two state elections.
"We are determined to live up to the historic challenges our country is facing," Merz said, referring to the coalition between his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
Merz's position has come under mounting pressure after Sunday's election results. In the north-eastern Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes, with the CDU failing to reach the threshold to stay in the state parliament.
Meanwhile in Berlin, the CDU came second to the hard-left Die Linke party, with the AfD also making significant gains.
Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow" for the centre-left CDU.
"This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he acknowledged.
He however said there had been no discussion about his own position since the results and pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings alone were behind the election defeats.
"I know that I as an individual played a role in these state elections," Merz said, before adding: "But the reasons for the results go far beyond just me."
"We are witnessing a profound transformation of Germany's political party system, as is happening in many other countries around the world."
There have been rumours Merz, who has only been in power for 16 months, could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap due to his poor approval ratings.
Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave."
The two elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU fell short of a 5% threshold to enter parliament, underperforming against what had already been projected to be the party's worst ever result in the area. Merz earlier conceded that this result was "a disaster".
While the AfD won the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it is unlikely to govern as other parties may refuse to work with it.
Some branches of the party are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.
But its anti-immigration, Germany first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.
In Berlin, the CDU's defeat means Die Linke, which won the most votes, could now take power in a coalition.

81facb5b38cd.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/main-kremlin-party-keeps-control-of-russian-parliament-after-a-carefully-orchestrated-vote Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Main Kremlin party keeps control of Russian parliament after a carefully orchestrated vote World Sep 21, 2026 10:17 AM EDT The main Kremlin party retained its majority in Russia's parliament, election officials said Monday, after three days of carefully orchestrated balloting that excluded most opposition candidates and helped President Vladimir Putin maintain his tight grip on power. Preliminary results indicated that United Russia would get 355 out of 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower chamber of parliament, the Central Election Commission said, which would be a record high for the party if confirmed. READ MORE: Russia wraps up first wartime parliamentary election with Kremlin dominance all but assured Results from over 95% of the polling stations gave United Russia just under 58% of the vote for the 225 seats apportioned by parties, according to commission chair Ella Pamfilova. Another 225 lawmakers were chosen to represent individual constituencies, and the results showed United Russia candidates leading in 208 of those races. A handful of seats will go to candidates who ran without a party affiliation in single-seat races, according to preliminary results. It was the first parliamentary election since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the first to include residents of four regions of that country that were seized and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year. At a polling station in the Russian-held part of the Donetsk region, voters dropped their ballots in a box under the gaze of an armed Russian soldier. READ MORE: Russian election observer loses consciousness during arrest by police, opposition party says Voting also was held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal. The government was "able to carry out the campaign and the voting the way it wanted, with the most optimal output," said Tatyana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, in an online commentary. The election followed a crackdown on dissent The Kremlin tightened its crackdown on opposition before the election, including barring Russia's only liberal, anti-war party from the ballot and allowing it to compete only in single-constituency races. The Kremlin has sought the parliamentary election to showcase popular support for the war, and strove to avoid political risks by stamping out any dissent. A massive state media campaign and tight control over the election in the absence of genuine opposition left little doubt that the Kremlin will keep tight control of Russian politics as economic costs rise and Ukrainian drone attacks increase deep inside the country. READ MORE: Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones at Russia, including 'largest ever' attack on Moscow Electronic balloting was available in many regions and encouraged by authorities. Critics said it made it easier for the government to control the outcome of the vote. Pamfilova said turnout was just over 59% — the most for a parliamentary election in over a decade. The final results will be announced Friday, she said. Criticism of the war was silenced The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to publicly criticize the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia's Supreme Court, and only has a few dozen candidates in the single-constituency races. Additionally, some anti-war politicians were imprisoned or forced to flee abroad ahead of the campaign. Yabloko and the Communist Party, which has criticized some aspects of government policy but carefully avoided any criticism of Putin, said many of their observers were turned away from polling stations. Russia didn't invite observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, with the Foreign Ministry accusing the group of "double standards" for its criticism of the country. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons said the decision was a breach of Russia's commitments as a member state of the organization. Ukrainian attacks bring the war home The election took place against the backdrop of incessant Ukrainian drone attacks. On Sunday, Russia's Defense Ministry reported that it downed 1,110 Ukrainian drones overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said hundreds of drones targeted the capital and described it as "the largest ever" attack on the city. The Moscow Oil Refinery was hit, he said, and so was another building. Three people were killed in the wider Moscow region, Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. A total of 38 others were injured and received medical treatment, according to the Health Ministry. Ukraine's long-range drone strikes over the summer pounded oil refineries, triggering a widespread fuel crisis, and set ablaze sprawling warehouses of online retailers Wildberries and Ozon, bringing the war home for millions of Russians like never before. "Putin, of course, will interpret United Russia's results as confirmation of the (public) support of the war, even though it is not the case: the overall demand for ending the war is growing," said Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center. "The main question is: what now? There are great concerns about mobilization, new repressions, harsher measures, and escalation," she wrote. Brain imaging could reveal early changes linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
MRI scans show that the thickness of the outermost layer of the brain changes before the onset of the disease, detectable up to seven years prior, researchers reported August 19 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the differences are too subtle to use as a diagnostic tool, they could help researchers understand the early stages of Alzheimer’s.
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia and can cause memory loss, disorientation and behavior shifts. But changes in the brain can occur long before these cognitive symptoms appear. Sticky protein fragments called amyloid-beta build up in the brains of people who go on to develop Alzheimer’s. These bundles, along with tangles of another protein called tau, slowly kill off brain cells and shrink the brain.
Under the current criteria, spotting A-beta buildups via positron emission tomography scans, or PET scans, is enough for an Alzheimer’s diagnosis even in the absence of cognitive symptoms. But most people do not receive PET scans without symptoms, so they won’t get diagnosed until later.
To better understand how the disease takes shape, Alzheimer’s researcher Yunpeng Wang and colleagues wanted to test whether they could spot brain changes before patients developed A-beta buildups.
The team examined MRI scans from over a thousand participants in long-term studies that track brain changes with aging. Wang and colleagues compared changes in the thickness of the cortex — the outermost layer of the brain, which averages around 2.5 millimeters thick— between people who later showed high A-beta levels and people who did not.
People who went on to develop high A-beta levels had thicker cortices than people who did not. Differences in thickness of a few hundredths of a millimeter were visible up to seven years before the participants were deemed to have high A-beta levels based on their PET scans. The cortices of people in both groups thinned naturally with age, but those of people who later developed high A-beta thinned less overall. The researchers didn’t observe any link between the thickness of the cortex and memory problems at this early stage of the disease.
The findings imply that “the trajectory of cortical changes is not [as] simplistic as we used to think,” says Victor Montal, a degenerative diseases researcher at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center who was not involved in the work. Rather than assuming the cortex thins consistently due to atrophy as the disease progresses, researchers will need to account for slower thinning in the early stages when studying Alzheimer’s, he says.
The relative thickening of the cortex might come from inflammation that occurs as A-beta first starts to accumulate, says Wang, of the University of Oslo. But MRIs can’t determine the cause of the thickening directly.
“I don’t think that this cortical thickness is something you’re going to use clinically,” says Frederik Barkhof, a neuroradiologist at University College London who was not involved in the study. The changes in cortex thickness are too subtle to use as individual diagnostic tools, he says, but they could help researchers understand the mechanisms behind Alzheimer’s disease and emerging treatments.
For example, some existing Alzheimer’s treatments remove A-beta but don’t stop the volume loss in the brain. The new findings could indicate that the current treatments reduce inflammation and not that a patient is losing excess brain tissue despite treatment, he says.

d7dd7d74f5b6.text: Germany's ruling center-right party, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union, was shut out of a state parliament for the first time Sunday as the far-right Alternative for Germany scored its second victory this month. Why it matters: The result marks the third state election AfD has won — and its second this month — underscoring its growing strength even as Germany's other major parties refuse to govern with it. Driving the news: Merz, who has low approval ratings, told reporters that "reforms have to come." AfD won about 38% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the CDU recorded its worst result in any German state election since World War II. The CDU fell from 13% to 4.9% and lost all representation. In Berlin's state election, the Left more than doubled its vote share to 25.7% and finished first for the first time. Flashback: AfD won its first state election in Thuringia in 2024, though other parties kept it out of government because they refused to enter into a coalition. Earlier this month, it won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt, but fell just three seats short of a majority. It is now seeking enough outside support to form Germany's first far-right state government since World War II. Vice President JD Vance met with AfD's co-leader days before last year's federal election and told the Munich Security Conference there was "no room for firewalls," referring to mainstream parties' refusal to govern with the AfD. The big picture: Germany's political firewall against AfD is rooted partly in the country's post-World War II consensus against returning the far-right to government and has been reinforced by intelligence concerns about extremism within the party. Germany's domestic intelligence service continues to monitor AfD nationally as a suspected extremist organization. A court in February blocked the agency from classifying the entire party as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization while a broader case proceeds. The anti-migration party calls for " remigration " — large-scale deportations and encouraging immigrants to leave. It also wants to abandon the euro, lift Russian sanctions and end weapons deliveries to Ukraine. What they're saying: AfD leader Alice Weidel called on Merz to "face the consequences" of the CDU's losses and said her party had displaced the CDU as Germany's "people's party." She wrote on X the CDU "will have to think very carefully about whether it can continue with this firewall policy, especially in eastern Germany" and called for the parties to sit down for talks. The bottom line: AfD's rise is reshaping politics in Europe's largest economy, putting growing pressure on Germany's governing center and the firewall that has kept the party out of power.

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker.
The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them.
The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield.
At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began.
German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems.
He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks.
The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament.
Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well.
It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist.
The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past.
The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want.
Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party.
The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets.
High time for political change, says the AfD.
Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician.
Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party.
I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual.
Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted.
Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed.
He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required.
But German patience is running thin.
Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future.
Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped.
Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people.
Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology.
In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive".
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect.
Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy.
Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget.
When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable.
Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example.
This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech.
Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels.
The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and t

Google has been fined â¬403m (Â£345m) by the Republic of Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) over its handling of location data.
The penalty - one of the largest of its kind imposed by the Irish watchdog authority - followed an inquiry launched into the tech giant six years ago, following complaints from several European consumer rights organisations.
On Monday the DPC said its investigation found Google had processed data in a manner that was not "lawful", "fair" or "transparent".
The inquiry concerned Google's processing of location data in three specific features - Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy between 25 May 2018 to 4 February 2020.
Location data is any kind of data which can be used to infer a person's location.
It can "reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private", said DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle in a statement released on Monday.
The report said Google's practices "infringed" General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) - legislation that came into effect on 25 May, 2018, creating strict data privacy and security law within the European Union (EU).
Doyle added: "The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA (European Economic Area), and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner."
He continued: "As a result of Google's failures... individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data.
"The retention of users' location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control."
In addition to being fined, Google has also been ordered to bring its data processing into compliance within six months.
How have Google responded?
In a statement, Google said: "This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we've significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple."
They also said they have made data protection improvements in recent years, including "industry-first auto-delete controls", which enables all users to "set your account to automatically delete your data on a rolling three, 18, or 36-month basis".
Other measures to safeguard personal data have also been introduced, they said, such as "simple ads management", which allows you "to turn off personalized ads entirely", and "increased transparency", including "consolidated detailed information about our location data practices and account settings".

Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights
EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of how the service works, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.
The technical problem at Prestwick in Ayrshire caused disruption at airports across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, delaying dozens of flights.
Nats said a "connectivity issue" was to blame for the disruption, and that it had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick that led to the cancellation of 2,000 flights earlier in September.
The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity" although officials warned of knock-on effects.
A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".
According to aviation analytics company Cirium, as of 13:45 BST, at least 200 flights had been cancelled or did not fly on Monday. This includes 100 flights scheduled to arrive in the UK and 99 that were due to depart from the UK.
Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 47 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 11 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.
The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.
It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".
Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure".
Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership.
When asked by BBC Radio 4's World at One programme whether Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?"
Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure.
Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers.
British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing".
A Nats spokesperson apologised for the disruption, saying: "In the real world, we accept technology can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible.
"What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority."
They added that it was working to return air traffic to normal as quickly as possible and urged passengers to check their flight status with their airline.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the problems with flights were "deeply frustrating" for passengers.
Steve Davies, 74, told the BBC he was "cheesed off with air traffic control" as technical issues with its systems seemed to be "happening a lot".
He and his wife Sadie became stuck at Birmingham airport after being told to disembark their easyJet flight to Edinburgh on Monday morning.
Nicole McCloskey, from Kilmarnock, had been due to go to Disneyland Paris with her family before their flight was cancelled.
She told the BBC her family got a message to say the flight was delayed while they were travelling to Glasgow airport, but only found out it had been grounded altogether once they arrived.
Nicole said they have been rebooked on another flight on later on Monday and were hopeful "it's sorted in time".
Not much is known about what caused the latest Nats problems, except that there was a technical failure at its control centre in Prestwick, which looks after traffic across northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, catering for about 42% of the UK's air traffic.
The other Nats centre at Swanwick in Hampshire looks after airspace in the southern part of the UK, including the approaches to Heathrow and Gatwick.
The Swanwick incident last month affected hundreds of thousands of passengers, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas earlier this month.
That disruption was much more severe as it affected intercontinental and long-haul travel via UK airspace.
Nats said in a report last week that the software glitch happened "in the space of a millisecond" leading to the system producing corrupted data.
However, the fact that the UK's air traffic control system has suffered two significant issues in a short space of time has attracted a great deal of criticism, and the pressure on Nats boss Martin Rolfe - who insisted last week he would not resign - is only likely to mount.
Rolfe told the BBC at the time he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure".
"My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he said.

Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them.
Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait.
After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN.
"How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them."
As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen.
He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen â one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe â but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in.
In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast.
This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.
Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised UN-recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.
"We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee."
Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded.
Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old.
"What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically.
"It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere."
Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate.
Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi.
He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears.
"Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us."
How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014.
A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes.
Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed.
Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here."
His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first, then food, water and an education.
"As you see we just fled with our clothes, and left everything behind, because [in Yemen] there is no peace."

Almost two million people are under evacuation orders in Japan as Typhoon Dujuan batters a number of the country's prefectures.
Japan's Meteorological Agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life", but several warnings have now been downgraded, with the danger to life warning remaining in place in Oshima Town.
Strong winds caused power cuts for more than 50,000 people, while hundreds of flights have been cancelled and rail services have been suspended.
Dujuan has had sustained winds of 130km/h (80.8mph) and gusts of 194 km/h. It is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El NiÃ±o", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms.
The level three warnings, for heavy rain, and the level four warnings, for landslides have now been either downgraded or lifted by the Japan Meteorological Agency in most areas.
The level four warnings remain in Shinagawa Ward, Toshima Village, and Niijima Village.
Authorities have advised the public to pay attention to weather information.
Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, has hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events.
Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival have been cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, has also cancelled Monday's programme.
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has reportedly delayed her trip to the United States this week to monitor the effects of the typhoon.
She had been due in New York on Tuesday to meet with US President Donald Trump and speak at the UN General Assembly.
The Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman who lived in the house, aged in her 60s, may have been swept away and is believed to have been buried alive.
Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site.
The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital.
Firefighters in Kanagawa prefecture said they received a call from a man who reported his house had been crushed by a landslide.
Some research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions.
As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however.
Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds.
And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall.
This year, El NiÃ±o - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor.
El NiÃ±o doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit.
Some El NiÃ±o events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example.
The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday.
Additional reporting by Mark Poynting, climate reporter

f380e8940e59.text: President Trump over the weekend considered ordering a strike against the Houthis in Yemen before deciding to hold off for now, two U.S. officials said. Why it matters: Trump was caught between wanting to help his friend and ally, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and avoiding getting entangled on a new front in the Middle East. Catch up quick: Ten days ago, bin Salman (MBS) called Trump twice on the same day, urging him to launch strikes against the Houthis as the Iran-backed group closed in on a vital Red Sea chokepoint. Trump rejected the request and agreed only to help the Saudis with intelligence and targeting data. U.S. officials said at the time they wouldn't take military action as long as the Houthis did not interrupt non-Saudi ship traffic in the Red Sea. Several days later, U.S. diplomats met with Houthi officials and received assurances that the rebel group has no intention of closing the Bab-al-Mandeb Strait. Behind the scenes: But late last week the Saudis, who were having trouble pushing back on Houthi advances, again asked Trump to take military action in Yemen, the two U.S. officials said. They said that over the weekend Trump held consultations with his senior advisers about the possibility of strikes against the Houthis. One U.S. official said the commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Adm. Brad Cooper, prepared options for airstrikes in Yemen and presented them to Secretary of Defense Hegseth on Saturday. But Trump ultimately decided to hold off, another U.S. official said. The New York Times first reported about Trump's deliberations around the possible strike in Yemen. The White House and the Saudi embassy in Washington declined to comment. What they're saying: "The president changed his mind and did not want to open a Pandora's box by striking because it could cause the Houthis to hold the Bab-al-Mandeb at risk and create a second choke point," Alex Plitsas, a fellow at the Atlantic Council and former Pentagon official, told Axios. That "would cause oil prices to spike further when the Saudis were supposed to take the lead on dealing with the Houthi problem," he added. State of play: The Saudis, together with Yemeni government forces, have been working for two weeks on a counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, but it has been delayed several times, sources say. In the meantime, the Houthis have been escalating strikes against Saudi Arabia. Over the weekend, they launched a missile toward Riyadh.

For the first time, scientists have spotted radio waves from an exoplanet.
Astronomer Yvette Cendes knows what you’re thinking: “When people see ‘radio signal from an exoplanet,’ they think aliens,” she says. But, sorry — it’s not aliens.
Instead, it could be the first clear evidence of an aurora on a planet outside the solar system, Cendes and colleagues report in a paper submitted September 15 to arXiv.org. The radio waves also reveal the planet’s magnetic field, making this potentially the first direct detection of the magnetic field of an exoplanet.
“This result, if it holds up in peer review, is an incredibly exciting advancement,” says astronomer Joe Callingham of the University of Amsterdam, who was not involved with the research. “It would be a fantastic result.”
Using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, scientists observed radio waves from Beta Pictoris b, a gas giant orbiting a young star about 63 light-years away. Importantly, the researchers were able to trace those radio waves to the exoplanet itself, rather than the star that it orbits. “We can rule out the star, and … we can say that it’s from this one particular planet,” says Cendes, of the University of Oregon in Eugene. That’s been a major hurdle for previous efforts to find radio waves from exoplanets.
Auroras are the source of Earth’s northern lights, and they also occur on other planets in the solar system, including Saturn, Jupiter and Mars. They’re caused by electrically charged particles circling in a planet’s magnetic field, exciting molecules in the atmosphere that generate the glow. As the charged particles circle, they emit radio waves. Auroras emit radio waves that are circularly polarized, which means that the orientation of the waves rotates in a circle. And that’s what the researchers saw from Beta Pictoris b.
Because auroras depend on magnetic fields, measuring the radio waves from them can reveal information about the planet’s magnetic field. Beta Pictoris b, the researchers found, has a magnetic field of more than 1,000 gauss — a common unit of magnetism. Earth’s magnetic field is tiny in comparison, about half a gauss. “It’s an incredibly, incredibly strong magnetic field, much stronger than anything in our solar system,” Cendes says.
That’s not surprising for a large planet like Beta Pictoris b, which has a mass 10 times that of Jupiter. Its large mass means it’s close in size to brown dwarfs, which are in a class of their own — too big to be planets and too small to be stars. Scientists have previously seen auroras on brown dwarfs, which indicate magnetic fields of thousands of gauss. So, such a whopping magnetic field on a large planet is not unexpected.
To really clinch the case for an aurora on an exoplanet, Callingham says, you’d want to see the radio waves pulsate in time. That’s because the aurora should rotate in and out of view as the planet spins — roughly once every eight hours for Beta Pictoris b. “So TBD, but, compelling,” Callingham says. “It’s probably auroral.”

d66934ac8d83.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-grand-conspiracy-probe-presses-on-with-subpoenas-after-the-lead-prosecutors-exit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's 'grand conspiracy' probe presses on with subpoenas after the lead prosecutor's exit Politics Sep 21, 2026 11:49 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Before taking over the sprawling Justice Department investigation into foes of President Donald Trump, Joe diGenova decried the lack of progress in bringing indictments. Five months later, diGenova has left his position without charging a single case, clouding the future of an investigation that has animated right-wing commentators eager to prove an ill-defined theory of a "deep state" conspiracy to take down the Republican president. READ MORE: Prosecutor brought in to lead investigation of Trump foes tells AP that he has resigned Justice Department officials are pressing forward despite diGenova's departure, with a flurry of subpoenas to former law enforcement and intelligence officials expected to yield grand jury testimony in the weeks ahead at the Fort Pierce, Florida, home court of a favored Trump-appointed federal judge. Yet whether anyone ultimately will be charged, and for what, remains an open question. Investigators face not only legal hurdles and personnel upheaval but an impatient White House after more than a year of fits and starts. The investigation known familiarly as the "grand conspiracy" case is the clearest example yet of the Trump administration's efforts to leverage law enforcement powers to enact retribution on the president's adversaries. The tumult that has defined the probe exposes a familiar gap between White House demands for speedy action and the Justice Department's ability to craft the president's litany of grievances into a prosecutable case. DiGenova's departure injects fresh uncertainty into the investigation The investigation has always been a tough task, aiming to knit together separate FBI probes of Trump — including related to Russian election interference and his retention of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida — into a coherent narrative of a government conspiracy. Prior efforts to investigate the investigators have failed to uncover the kind of criminal misconduct the conspiracy probe aims to prove. "The idea of connecting all those different investigations into one single conspiracy, there's no basis for that," retired federal prosecutor Randall Eliason said. "Then, maybe more importantly, there's no basis for an allegation that any one of them was actually a criminal act against Trump. They've all been verified and upheld in one way or another." If the mandate is unusual, so, too, was the person picked to lead it. READ MORE: Attorney General Blanche blurs Justice Department boundaries by appearing at political events DiGenova, who's 81, was a top prosecutor in President Ronald Reagan's administration but had been out of government for decades. He made headlines in 2020 after he said a cybersecurity official who attested to the legitimacy of the election Trump lost to Democrat Joe Biden should be "drawn and quartered." DiGenova apologized after being sued. A prominent booster of the theory that Trump was victimized by a "deep state" conspiracy, diGenova was appointed in April shortly after Trump ousted Pam Bondi as attorney general after she struggled to prosecute his foes. The appointment was heralded by Trump allies who regard the probe as a long-awaited reckoning for former officials they believe wronged the president. Attorney General Todd Blanche, who took the reins of the department after Bondi's firing, also trumpeted diGenova's arrival, writing on social media: "Welcome to the fight, Joe!" By Sept. 10, diGenova was gone amid Trump administration frustration with the pace and management of the probe. His parting comments suggested he didn't see a pathway for imminent indictments. "If you want indictments where there's no evidence, you have an ethical problem," he told the New York Post. DiGenova told The Associated Press those comments were taken out of context, adding: "There's plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can't do that." DiGenova was sworn in days after a career national security prosecutor, Maria Medetis Long, was removed from the investigative team after conveying concerns about an investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan. A lawyer for Brennan has seized on the upheaval, pointing to the departures as proof that prosecutors who have assessed the evidence have been unpersuaded and pushed aside by a Justice Department angling for indictments at all costs. "I've spent decades in and around the Justice Department. I've never even conceived of a situation like this," attorney Ken Wainstein said, in which the Justice Department is "blatantly trying to frame somebody for a crime that is complete fiction." He made the comments to a judge last week as he put prosecutors on notice that he intended to attack any indictment of Brennan on the grounds of vindictive prosecution. The Justice Department has not announced a replacement for diGenova, but a team of prosecutors and agents remains at work, including Kurt Olsen, an attorney who unsuccessfully pushed the Justice Department in 2020 to back Trump's false election fraud claims. Trump has long cast himself as the victim of a 'deep state' conspiracy As the Justice Department reeled last year from the bungled handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, officials eager to change the topic announced a new investigation and a directive from Bondi, then the attorney general, to present evidence before a

e6c5d419ee4c.text: Americans are "connecting the dots" between climate and affordability strain, Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) said Monday at an Axios House event on the sidelines of Climate Week and the UN General Assembly. Why it matters: But as pocketbook issues dominate a critical midterm race, Schatz says that doesn't mean the first thing he mentions to constituents is climate. Still, climate-tangent conversations — like utility prices and the data center boom — are looming over the polls. Driving the news: "I think we should talk about climate in the context of people not being able to afford their lives," Schatz told Axios' Ben Geman, pointing to insurance non-renewals, soaring gas prices and rising utility bills . "It's not that difficult anymore for us to be able to say, look, one of the reasons things are getting more expensive is we're not addressing the climate crisis," he said, criticizing the federal government's renewables roadblocks. "The climate imperatives used to have to be balanced against people's pocketbooks, and now they are perfectly lined up," he added. "We do not have to make trade-offs. They are deciding to make the planet worse and make your pocketbook situation worse." Catch up quick: Schatz has been a leading congressional voice on climate issues, representing a heavily petroleum -dependent U.S. state with high energy prices that's at particular risk from the impacts of climate change. The state has taken on an ambitious clean energy initiative that aims for 100% renewable energy by 2035 on the neighbor islands, including Maui and Hawaiʻi. Friction point: The sweeping GOP budget bill signed into law by President Trump last year phased out wind, solar, and electric vehicle subsidies that the prior administration championed as tools to bolster clean tech. It's one front in Trump's broader rollback of Biden-era climate policies , including moves to kill regulations and a slowdown in permitting of renewables projects. In particular, administration officials have targeted wind power, which Trump has repeatedly criticized. Still, the AI boom is expected to drive a surge in clean energy this year. A Rwandan man, who has been living in north London, has become the first person charged in the UK with offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide against the Tutsi, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has said.
Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, has been charged with one offence of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity.
Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Brown "is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others".
Brown will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.
Ferguson said the decision to charge Brown was made "after reviewing a file of evidence submitted by the War Crimes Team at the Metropolitan Police".
"We concluded that our legal test for bringing criminal charges had been met," he added.
The War Crimes Team began their investigation in September 2019 after a formal request from the Rwandan government to investigate people allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994.
The Metropolitan Police said the charges follow "a complex and extensive seven-year investigation".
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes.
"The War Crimes Teams remains committed to ensuring those suspected of involvement in genocide and other atrocity crimes are held accountable through due legal process.
"A number of other investigations remain ongoing into other individuals in the UK for similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda."

Andyâs view
In Mao Zedongâs 1938 essay On Protracted War, penned during the Japanese invasion of China, he divided conflict into three phases: strategic defense, strategic stalemate, and strategic counter-offensive.
On the eve of a leadersâ summit this week in Washington, US-China ties are stuck in the stalemate stage, deadlocked on everything from trade and technology to Taiwan â and itâs only a matter of time before hostilities ramp back up.
Of course, thereâs the mercurial Trump factor, which throws off any tidy analysis. The US president plans to personally greet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Andrews Air Base this week â an honor normally reserved for popes and close partners â and has been conciliatory to Beijing ahead of these talks. But Trump could just as easily flip, perhaps if Republicans are routed in Novemberâs midterms, as he did at the end of his first term when he blamed China and COVID-19 â âkung-fluâ â for his election defeat.
And stalemate isnât quite the same thing as a truce. Beneath the diplomatic surface, the two sides are radically at odds over just about everything: Beijingâs role in providing a financial (and, reportedly, tactical) lifeline for Iran as it lashes out at its Gulf neighbors and the US; keeping Russiaâs economy afloat as it pummels Ukraine; tariffs, sanctions, currency levels, student visas, and much more. Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary running point on the summit, once likened the superpowersâ relationship to a game of water polo: Above the water, the two teams toss the ball back and forward; below, legs kick and flail.
But in a stalemate, the most awkward problems either get ignored or deferred. Trumpâs extravagant welcome gesture will almost certainly be matched by prosaic summit outcomes. A Financial Times headline summed up the low expectations: âThe main Trump-Xi summit achievement will be it happening at all.â
A case in point is the activation of the Board of Trade, an arrangement agreed upon at the leadersâ meeting in Busan, South Korea, that is explicitly designed to avoid the tough issues. China is demanding the US ease export bans on high-tech goods, like chipmaking gear; the US bitterly complains about Chinese overproduction and transhipment. The trade board, however, limits itself to ânon-sensitiveâ consumer products â flip flops, toys, and kitchenware.
On AI safety â arguably the most significant topic on the agenda, given the risks of an AI-induced blow-up (CNN reports a recent close call involving a Chinese ship in the Middle East, wrongly identified by a US chatbot to be carrying nuclear material) â it isnât even clear the two sides are talking about the same thing. In the US, AI safety refers to existential risk; in China, it means preserving regime stability.
As always, Xiâs priority is saving the party that he leads â thatâs why he was selected for the job â and a good summit outcome would be simply prolonging the superpower standoff, at least until a party gathering next year thatâs expected to hand him a fourth five-year term in office. To borrow Maoâs parlance, Xiâs not ready yet for the strategic counter-offensive stage.
Among the proposals put forward by the Trump administration is a regular AI dialogue, alongside setting up something akin to an AI crisis hotline. The offer is perhaps unintentionally symbolic of the countriesâ stasis â limited in scope and ambition even as they grapple with huge geopolitical and societal instability.
Itâs even unclear whether an AI hotline mechanism would work. Decades ago, their militaries installed a telephone link to be used in the event of an emergency. One arrived in 2001 when a US spy plane limped into Hainan Island with a 24-member crew after a collision with a Chinese fighter jet that killed its pilot. The American side made a frantic call: Nobody picked up.
Notable
- China holds âescalation dominanceâ over the US when it comes to economic conflict, but that âwould not spare its own economy pain if it were forced into a tit-for-tat conflict with Washington,â Adam Posen argued in Foreign Affairs.

452d6a56fc54.text: OpenAI on Monday released international AI safety standards as world leaders, namely the U.S. and China, weigh how to mitigate risk. Why it matters: The U.S. approach to coordinating on AI risk with China will be heavily informed by industry recommendations. Driving the news: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng over the weekend discussed a U.S.-China AI dialogue to notify the other country when AI incidents reached national security risk levels. The devil is in the details and OpenAI is proposing solutions that CEO Sam Altman will cover in his address at the United Nations Security Council in New York on Wednesday. What they're saying: OpenAI recommends leveraging AI safety institutes around the world to facilitate standard-setting through the U.S. Center for AI Security and Innovation, which is part of the Commerce Department. The company also recommends shared global measurements for classifying incidents and how to track, report and respond to alignment issues. The goal is to have international standards for incidents that happen before deployment in test settings and those that occur in the real world, an OpenAI official told Axios. What we're watching: Expect AI labs to continue chiming in as all eyes are on President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's meetings and a state dinner featuring industry heavy hitters later this week.

It's a very inexpensive price to pay for what we've done," Trump said of the war, which he describes as critical to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. "Remember that. It's a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more." 'Gas prices matter,' Republican strategist says Despite what Trump says, there are few things that may matter more this election year than the price of a gallon of gasoline, according to political operatives in both parties. "Gas prices matter because they're one of the few economic indicators voters experience and see in real time," said veteran Republican strategist Chris Wilson. "The price is literally staring them in the face several times a week. So I wouldn't minimize the frustration we're seeing, particularly among working- and middle-class voters." Interviews with voters this week found bipartisan frustration and disappointment. Democrats and independents were especially motivated to punish Republicans at the ballot box for their economic hardship, while some of Trump's working-class supporters pledged to support Republicans this fall, even if they weren't happy with the president's leadership on the economy. Some Republicans say they're disappointed Dan Lloyd, who voted for Trump, lamented the president's leadership as the 63-year-old carpenter paid $4.39 a gallon to fill up his pickup truck in Mesa, Arizona. "He hurt himself stepping into this," Lloyd said of Trump. "Where's all this oil from Venezuela? I thought we were flush with gas and everything, but no. The American people eat it every time, whether it's interest rates, food, gasoline." Still, he expects to vote Republican in the midterms. "I think the Democratic Party has lost its way," Lloyd said. "I just feel like the whole system's on the verge of collapse." In sweltering Edinburg, Texas, 52-year-old Kristin Jimenez shrugged off the rising price of gas after filling up her Mercedes. "We've paid the same price under Republican presidents, we've paid this price under Democrat presidents," said Jimenez, a mother who runs a small business. "We don't mind paying $8 for a cup of coffee at Starbucks, but we have a problem paying four bucks at the pump?" she said. "Make it make sense." More than 1,500 miles to the north in central Michigan, 35-year-old Garth Johnson is trying to make ends meet running a deep-cleaning business with several gas-powered vehicles and one machine fueled by diesel, which was $6.79 a gallon as he filled up his SUV. This London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs.
The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us".
Creative director SeÃ¡n McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses.
Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers.
Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth".
Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026:
Messy girl aesthetic
"The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season.
She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quite luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year.
Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion.
She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy".
This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives.
Gardening-core
According to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world.
A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower.
"There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats.
It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu.
Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show.
Modern goddess
Whilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film.
Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer.
Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes".
Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics.
Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide.
"Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes.
Orange
Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year.
Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and TimothÃ©e Chalamet's matching neon outfits , externalat the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway.
Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days.
Ballet
Ever the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet.
After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year.
Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall.
"Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel.
"Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

Paramount Skydance has settled a lawsuit with dozens of US states, removing a major hurdle to its $110bn (Â£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta told a news conference that state officials agreed to terms after securing commitments to protect competition across film and television, and broadcasting.
Still, "the settlement is not a vote of support for this merger," Bonta said. "I don't think these two companies should merge."
Paramount chief executive David Ellison hailed the resolution, saying: "Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and - most importantly -the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling."
In a statement, Ellison said that now the state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America concerns had been addressed, "we have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action".
Ellison had previously threatened to move studio operations out of California.
The settlement will help boost film production in the US, Bonta said, adding that under the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year.
To prevent the studio from fulfilling its 30-movie annual quota with low-budget or automated content, Bonta said there are strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films.
Officials wanted to guarantee "real, robust movies" that generate economic activity and put people back to work, he added.
Though Ellison previously indicated the merged company would keep its headquarters in California for the foreseeable future, Bonta clarified that this commitment was not written into the legal agreement.
"It's not part of the deal," Bonta said.
To ensure remaining terms are enforced, Paramount has agreed to the appointment of an independent monitor to oversee ongoing compliance with the settlement.
California led the legal push alongside a coalition of state attorneys general from Arizona, Colorado, and New Jersey.
Under the deal's initial terms, Paramount must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising over 30% over the following three years.
While mergers typically lead to corporate overlap and redundancies, Bonta maintained that it would be a "job creator" that will put people back to work across the industry.
Thanks to the deal, Bonta said that economic activity would be "$300m to $1.5bn more, at minimum, for film and TV production right here in our country".
"Importantly, that is the baseline. That is the minimum," Bonta said, noting that production commitments could surge by up to 700% if Congress passes a federal film tax credit.

0c9314bee4cc.text: What do a White House ban on journalists, a 250-foot arch near the nation's capital and Greenland have in common? President Trump needs all of them for national security purposes, he and his administration have argued. Why it matters: As he's unilaterally shattered presidential norms, Trump has justified his sweeping policy priorities with a familiar two-word rationale: national security. Driving the news: On the morning that the three banned outlets (CNN, MS NOW and Politico) sued the administration , Trump claimed that "FAKE NEWS" is "a threat to our National Security." It's not the first time the administration has said its press restrictions were a national security must: That was also part of the reasoning for new rules for Pentagon reporters , a war on leakers and subpoenas of journalists. National security purposes are a broad bucket that the president has also used to justify his D.C. redesign: Trump pitched his proposed " triumphal arch " as a dual-use facility housing snipers, drones and ammunition storage "for National Security purposes." That's also why the president was adamant his White House ballroom project must proceed (after he demolished the East Wing). The White House declined to comment beyond the president's post. Zoom out: The national security rationale has also fueled the administration's deregulatory AI approach. Earlier this month, Justice Department attorneys argued that laws that get in the way of a growing AI industry "threaten national security" in a statement of interest backing AI companies in The New York Times' copyright infringement lawsuit. What they're saying: The executive's use of national security as a justification for policy can trigger "extreme deference" in the courts, says Kimberly Wehle, a University of Baltimore law professor. Wehle notes the expanded executive power seen in Trump 2.0 has its origins in the Bush-era advancement of the unitary executive theory — though the national psyche today does not necessarily reflect the urgency of the 9/11 era. "It appears that the Trump administration has taken a page from that era and understands that it's easier to justify power from the standpoint of the public, and even in the courts, if you can say it's in the interest of national security," she says. Friction point: The argument hasn't always found a receptive audience. An appeals court considering Trump's White House ballroom project concluded last month that "[w]hile this court accords great weight and deference to invocations of national security and the safety of the President, such arguments are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card." Elizabeth Goitein, senior director of the Brennan Center's Liberty and National Security Program, says the ambiguity of "national security" has moved "toward this dangerous zone where the words … become a blank check" and "take on this talismanic significance in the courts." Trump didn't start it, she says. But "Trump's willingness to claim national security for things that so patently have nothing to do with national security is at a new level." Worth noting: The administration has also busted norms in the more traditional national security realm. After months of demanding U.S. ownership of Greenland as a national security necessity, Trump announced last week that the U.S. struck a deal with Denmark and Greenland to give America "permanent control over security" on the island, where the U.S. already had military access. South of the border, the administration has waged a year-long campaign against alleged narcoterrorists, killing some 230 people in boat strikes and fueling broad international law concerns. And while immigration policy is a key pillar of the nation's security apparatus, Trump's far-reaching crackdown has lumped international students , Temporary Protected Status holders and travelers from certain designated nations together under the guise of national security threats. The bottom line: National security concerns have long been fuel for the expansion of presidential authority. Trump, however, has used national security to justify acting not only as the commander in chief, but, recently, as a builder in chief and editor in chief as well. 68d3a5683f15.text: By — Andrew Dalton, Associated Press Andrew Dalton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/must-see-exhibits-at-george-lucass-new-museum-of-narrative-art-in-la Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Must-see exhibits at George Lucas's new Museum of Narrative Art in LA Arts Sep 21, 2026 2:17 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — "Star Wars" creator George Lucas called his Lucas Museum of Narrative Art a "temple to the people's art" and a project that "almost broke my will." Seventeen years after it was first envisioned, it will be opening to the public on Tuesday in Los Angeles. The $1 billion institution in Exposition Park near his alma mater the University of Southern California has become a life's work for him and his wife and co-founder, businesswoman Mellody Hobson. Its galaxies of galleries are filled almost entirely with their own collections. The 82-year-old Lucas has a love of doing things that are supposed to be impossible. The project was first conceived for San Franciso and Chicago and reached the initial design phase in both cities before Lucas was "kicked out," as he put it. The Los Angeles museum mixes the work of populist painters, commercial illustrators and comic artists with the kind of fine artists more associated with major museums. Here's a look at five things to make sure to see on a visit. Life-size Star Wars props and characters are displayed at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art before it opens to the public in Los Angeles, California, U.S. September 2, 2026. Photo by Mike Blake/REUTERS Slay, princess In the considerable green space that surrounds the museum, visitors will see statuary that includes a sculpture of Carrie Fisher's Princess Leia in her metal bikini choking Jabba the Hutt to death, a scene from 1983's "Return of the Jedi." Titled "The Hutt Slayer" and commissioned for the space, it's one of a handful of inevitable nods to "Star Wars" in and around the museum, but that faraway galaxy represents just a small fraction of its holdings and initial exhibits. The inaugural "Star Wars in Motion" exhibit shows vehicles used in the original trilogy and the Lucas-directed prequels. A Naboo starfighter hangs in a more permanent spot in the lobby of its library. A stroll on the paths through the grass will also bring views of statues of Yoda, Grogu, and Natalie Portman's Padmé Amidala. Banksy artwork at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art before it opens to the public in Los Angeles, California, U.S. September 2, 2026. Photo by Mike Blake/REUTERS Banksy, high above the street The museum is full of paintings from artists like Norman Rockwell who have long been considered the opposite of cool. But it has no lack of younger, hipper content. In a not-easy-to-find fifth-floor gallery are two walls of stenciled murals from the elusive and apparently recently "unmasked" British street artist Banksy, who worked personally with Lucas on his contributions to the institution. The work, whose presence was announced in the final weeks before the museum's opening, includes the familiar image of a girl releasing a heart-shaped balloon. Nearby are activist murals from artists including Judith Baca and Diego Rivera. Don't forget to look up at the oculus Architect Ma Yansong's big, billowing building almost seems to hover around and envelop the surrounding structures, including the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. He has likened it to a cloud, and perhaps its signature spot is an opening in that cloud, an oculus in the center of the dome above the main plaza that looks almost celestial. Ma told The Associated Press the spot is "almost like a spiritual space." "I think architecture is a narrative, is storytelling," he said. "The plaza, the oculus, the roof, different atmospheres that we provided, I think it's very important that the building become an emotional space for people." The exterior and entrance to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art before it opens to the public in Los Angeles, California, U.S. September 2, 2026. Photo by Mike Blake/REUTERS A rare but familiar Frida Kahlo self-portrait A Frida Kahlo portrait hung in a prominent spot in the museum's fourth-floor galleries will look as familiar to many visitors as some of the surrounding superhero art. But that belies how special it is. It may alone make a visit worth it for her devotees. The 1940 "Autorretrato Dedicado al Dr. Eloesser," or "Self Portrait Dedicated to Dr. Eloesser," was acquired by the Lucas Museum in 2020, and became one of the few such portraits from the artist held outside her native Mexico. READ MORE: 4 things to know about Obama's new presidential museum It shows her with a bloom of flowers in her hair, wearing a thorn necklace with drops of blood, and silver earrings that were a gift from Pablo Picasso, whose work is also in the museum collection. Soon after the museum acquired it in 2020, the director at the time told the Los Angeles Times she considered it "The Mona Lisa of Mexico." The painting is dedicated to Leo Eloesser, a San Francisco Bay Area physician who helped Kahlo with her chronic pain. A banner across the bottom calls him "mi médico y mi mejor amigo" — my doctor and my best friend. Dogs playing poker show the museum's high and low cards In a perfect encapsulation of the museum's merger of high and low art, just a few steps from the Kahlo portrait is Cassius Marcellus Coolidge's 1894 "Poker Game," which shows a group of dogs playing cards. Often considered the height of lowbrow, kitschy barroom art, it's the first in a series of 18 oil paintings on the theme from the American artist. It gets a new, elevated view in a museum that specializes in it. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
