Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.
Prime Minister Mindaugas SinkeviÄius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.
He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.
Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.
"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," SinkeviÄius told the BBC.
"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."
SinkeviÄius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".
It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.
The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.
"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."
Moscow did not comment on the incident.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.
Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.
Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.
Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform.
In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino explains the independent process would "recommend potential improvements".
Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened".
This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives".
Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash.
In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you", and says the consultation will be with confederations, member associations and "relevant stakeholders".
He insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!"
His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not."
Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be."
He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together".
Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves.
FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.
Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football.
"We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association," he adds in the letter.
"What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided.
"The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead."
Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE.
Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.
Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents.
Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.
Infantino's tone shift represents change in bid to survive - analysis
Having defiantly clung to power for weeks amid an unprecedented rebellion over his presidency, this is a significant change in tone from Infantino - and the first sign that he may feel he has no choice but to compromise if he is to win another re-election in March.
On 15 October, the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since this crisis began, and Infantino will no doubt hope that this relieves some of the pressure he is under.
But even if he is prepared to accept some changes to the way Fifa is run, will that be enough to win over some of those that have turned against him? Much may depend on the precise terms of reference for the external review that Infantino has proposed. After all, Infantino has not yet agreed to a similar review into his FFE plan.
As well as wanting him to step down, many of Infantino's critics want an overhaul of Fifa's governance, with curbs on the president's power (such as a maximum of a single term in office), more separation between the president and the Fifa administration, greater emphasis on human rights and sustainability, and the redistribution of Fifa's cash reserves.
It will be fascinating to see if Infantino is prepared to accept such changes if it means staying in power.

Major US television networks suspended their pooled coverage of President Donald Trump on Monday in response to CNN, Politico and MS NOW being barred from the White House.
Trump announced the ban on Friday as he accused the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. The companies said their reporters were denied access to the building on Saturday.
The three US outlets have since said they will sue the Trump administration in a bid to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".
Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.
Several other US outlets have also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday.
It meant there was no network TV footage of Trump boarding Air Force One or arriving in New York to attend the UN general assembly.
Trump also took part in a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new Marine One helipad on the White House South Lawn. The event was streamed on the White House site but his comments were inaudible.
The president did later appear on television following a meeting with the Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani. He told the president that all members of the media would be welcome at the press conference.
Trump said: "It's interesting because, they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press."
The pool involves media organisations sharing material to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.
Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of Trump.
The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place".
The three media organisations banned from the White House filed a lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington.
A joint statement announcing the legal action said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

A Sri Lankan court is set to rule on Naufer Moulavi, who is accused of masterminding the Easter bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500 in 2019.
Twenty-three others will also receive verdicts for their involvement in planning and carrying out the co-ordinated suicide bombings.
The attacks on several locations including several churches holding Easter mass and three luxury hotels was the deadliest attack Sri Lanka had seen since the end of its civil war in 2009.
The associates and relatives of nine suicide bombers are among those facing more than 23,000 charges, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms.
The prosecution had named Moulavi as the main organiser of the attacks, and had submitted what they said was a voluntary confession to the court where he had admitted his role.
The court accepted the confession. However, Moulavi later told the three-judge bench hearing the case that he was not shown what he was signing and rejected the allegations against him.
More than 2,300 people gave evidence for the prosecution.
There were also 2,076 pieces of evidence, including explosives, swords and firearms.
In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities.
In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks.
Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions.
For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks.
The verdict on Tuesday comes as a separate investigation on former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists.
The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics.
Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations.
Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

A Canadian province is suing OpenAI over its alleged failure to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT prior to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.
The company has previously apologised for not flagging Jessie Van Rootselaar's account to law enforcement before the 18-year-old killed eight people, including six children, in February.
British Columbia attorney general Niki Sharma said the lawsuit, filed to a US federal court on Monday, raised questions about "the responsibilities of technology companies when they become aware of credible threats of serious violence".
Families of those killed or injured in the shooting have filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI.
Media reports revealed that Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT activity was flagged by OpenAI's safety team for references to gun violence months before the attack, but the company did not alert local authorities.
In April, OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman apologised to the families of the victims.
"I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement," Altman wrote in an open letter.
The BBC has requested comment from OpenAI regarding the latest lawsuit.
"To date, OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community," Sharma said in a statement.
"The company still has an opportunity to demonstrate accountability by strengthening safeguards, improving transparency and taking concrete action to help prevent similar tragedies in the future."
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Sharma said she had not read the contents of the OpenAI chats.
"We have asked OpenAI to disclose these chats. They have refused. We should all be asking them: Why?" she said, according to CBC, external.
Sharma said the lawsuit was filed in California, as the alleged decision not to report the shooter's ChatGPT account occurred in that US state, according to AFP.
Sharma told reporters that any financial damages won by the province would go towards rebuilding the secondary school.

In a small green meadow in the Gredos mountains, west of Madrid, a couple of dozen cows belonging to Juan Ãngel Izquierdo and his family are grazing. The only noise is the gentle clang of the bells around the animals' necks.
This would be an idyllic scene were it not for the blackened pine and oak trees all around, the legacy of a devastating recent wildfire.
"It was immense, I've never seen anything like it," says Izquierdo, whose family have been farming here for 200 years.
The fire, in late July, merged with two others, burning a total of around 80,000 hectares (200,000 acres), making it the biggest blaze Spain has ever registered.
It consumed more than two-thirds of Izquierdo's land and killed 12 of his 85 cows. Another eight animals had to be put down because of their injuries. All the hay he had gathered to feed his cows in the winter was also burned.
"For us farmers, the summers are becoming more and more worrying, because they are getting hotter," he says. "It rains less, the wet season ends earlier and the autumn starts much later."
Wildfires
For farmers, such conditions are synonymous with fires.
"If you don't think about the wildfires too much, you feel okay," Izquierdo says. "But when a fire starts in a nearby village you start wondering â 'and what if we're next?'."
Wildfires are one of several symptoms of climate change which in recent years have had a substantial impact on Spain's economy, as well as contributing to shocking human tragedies.
World Weather Attribution, an international research organisation, found that the extreme conditions that drove record-breaking fires in Spain and Portugal in 2025 were 40 times more likely, external to happen due to the warming climate.
"The ultimate reason for the greater frequency and intensity of these kinds of fires has to be attributed to the increase in greenhouse gases caused mainly by the generalised use of fossil fuels," said Ernesto RodrÃguez Camino, president of the Spanish Meteorology Association.
The Socialist Prime Minister, Pedro SÃ¡nchez, has described the fires in dramatic terms, placing Spain in the front line of an environmental crisis.
"The climate emergency kills," he said in July, during a visit to the southern province of AlmerÃa where a wildfire claimed 15 lives.
This year, around 300,000 hectares of land have been burned in Spain, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), approximately half the total affected in the entire European Union.
In the last 40 years, damage caused by Spanish fires each year has exceeded 200,000 hectares on eight occasions â three of those since 2022.
Farming insurance association Agroseguro estimated that 16,000 hectares of crops had been destroyed by mid-August this year, a major blow for Spain's agri-food industry, which contributes 9% of the country's GDP.
The local authorities in Castilla y LeÃ³n, the region most heavily affected by this year's massive fire near Madrid, are offering compensation â between â¬5,500 ($6,300; Â£4,700) and â¬25,000 ($29,000; Â£21,000) to each farmer â depending on the damage suffered. But Izquierdo estimates that this will cover less than half of his losses.
Rising temperatures
For decades, Spain's warm climate has been a boon for one of its other biggest industries - tourism. Sun-drenched resorts along the Mediterranean coast, and in the Balearic and Canary Islands, have driven the country's growth as a tourist hub.
This year, close to 100 million foreigners are expected to come to Spain, making it the second most-visited country in the world, just behind France.
Yet there are signs that the heat is becoming too much for some travellers. A study by researchers at Madrid's Rey Juan Carlos University found that it can as a deterrent to potential visitors., external
"When there is a heatwave, the number of overnight stays drops in the destinations that we've studied, and there is also a drop in arrivals from some of Spain's biggest markets," says MarÃa Dolores SÃ¡nchez, an economist who co-authored the report.
"Tourism represents 13% of Spain's GDP, so this could have repercussions in the medium term when it comes to Spain's competitivity."
The medieval city of Toledo is on the plains of Castilla-La Mancha, far from Spain's coastline, but its rich history and winding streets have made it a popular destination for those seeking an alternative to the country's beaches and bars.
However, this summer tested their tolerance of heat, with the country registering a record-breaking 61 days of heatwaves that continued into early September. Toledo repeatedly saw temperatures in excess of 40C.
"It's quite difficult to do the tours in the summer," says guide Diego Esteban, of the company Visit Toledo. "We need to adapt, whether it is those of us who work in the tourism industry or the locals."
When leading tours in the summer months, Esteban makes sure that there are frequent stops, drinking water is provided and that the itineraries include plenty of shade. However, he would like to see more shade and drinking fountains available.
He says the heat has started to change the timing of the tourist season, bringing many more visitors during the cooler months of spring and autumn.
Warmer summers have also encouraged the so-called "coolcation" trend, whereby Spanish travellers seek out cooler areas to spend their holidays, typically in the north of the country.
Another consequence of Spain's warming climate has been drought. In 2024, after three years of minimal rainfall, the north-eastern region of Catalonia temporarily introduced stringent restrictions on water use, including a 25% reduction for industry and an 80% reduction for crop farming.

At least 11 people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey after an attacker opened fire before fleeing the scene.
The incident happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in Turkey's western province of Manisa at about 08:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Tuesday.
The attacker has since been detained, according to the local governor's office.
Local media reported that two of the victims taken to hospital were in critical conditions.
CCTV footage posted online appeared to show a male on a street near the school carrying a firearm, with other clips apparently showing him fleeing still carrying the weapon.
The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear.
It has been reported in Turkish media that the gunman is a 15-year-old student, though that has not been officially confirmed.
In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular".
It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa.

e4df3010c5c1.text: Of the various ways experts fear AI could kill us all , one is slowly moving closer to reality: AI learning to make itself unstoppable. Why it matters: Recursive Self Improvement, the ability of an AI model to build better versions of itself without human guidance, could make increasingly capable systems harder for humans to control. The RSI threshold doesn't represent danger by itself, but a lack of human control combined with rogue AI agents is a scenario that safety-conscious AI researchers have long feared. Driving the news : Researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI say the process of training new models has grown more automated, coming close to the RSI rubicon. An OpenAI employee told The Information the company has largely automated training new experimental models, with AI systems running experiments as directed by humans and correcting much of their work. Last week, Anthropic shared that its AI training is becoming more automated, with AI leading about 26% of Anthropic's R&D work. AI collaborates on 90% of work, the company says. "AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves," the company said. Reality check: Critics say the milestone is more a function of coding automation than a marker of impending doom or inevitable AI superpowers. While there's been an uptick in troubling AI security incidents in which models outstripped human control, some industry figures see those episodes as evidence of poor internal controls by OpenAI and other companies. Further evidence of that view emerged this week, when The Wall Street Journal reported that independent security researchers used Anthropic's Claude to break into OpenAI in July. Where does RSI come from? Flashback: The concept behind RSI emerged in the 1950s as artificial intelligence became an area of study. British mathematician and statistician Irving John Good described the idea in a 1965 paper : "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control." How RSI could lead to AI doom Threat level: Anthropic has warned RSI "might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems." Some researchers theorize that advanced AI could resist shutdown or modification if staying operational helped it accomplish its goals. Researchers into the hack by OpenAI agents into Hugging Face said the agents showed signs of this behavior. Another concern: Self-improving AI systems capable of copying themselves could create a kind of digital natural selection , favoring systems that are best at acquiring compute, money and power to grow fastest. In a darker version of this scenario, AI would be competing with humans for resources and power, experts say. Between the lines: Dangerous behavior might not stop with one generation of AI. Anthropic researchers found that some unwanted traits could pass from one model to another through training data, raising concerns that problematic behavior could persist across generations of AI. How close are we to RSI? The big picture: We're not there yet. A new analysis published this week found that AI feedback loops aren't yet hitting the RSI benchmarks. What we're watching: Attempts at building RSI. China's z.AI says they're heading toward RSI, where the models are helping build better infrastructure for better models. Google DeepMind researchers published a framework for "Dream-RSI," a system that recursively improves how an AI agent finds solutions. The bottom line: RSI isn't here yet, but it's a looming issue that's got the AI world on watch. Go deeper: AI's architects say the next era of human history is here

b812232a81b4.text: The race for AI supremacy between labs, companies and countries may be impossible to reconcile with the push for AI safety, industry insiders tell Axios. Why it matters: The top AI companies are proposing more independent oversight as they seek to engineer an AI slowdown . But trillions of dollars in incentives to keep pushing the frontier — and the money required for such scaling — will always loom larger, critics say. State of play: As AI CEOs pitch the public on self-policing mechanisms and the use of third-party evaluators to make sure their models behave, those same models are sharing less about how they respond to questions and come up with solutions to problems. The sheer complexity of AI systems, as well as the deployment of thousands of somewhat autonomous agents for a variety of tasks, will make real-time auditing or reviewing extremely difficult. There is a trust gap for independent safety groups due to concerns about close ties between the industry and some evaluators, as well as a shared pool of investors and funders in the AI research community. Follow the money: The incentive for speed is a lot more lucrative than the push to slow down in favor of safety. OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to go public at multi-trillion-dollar valuations, and the companies face pressure to offer incrementally better and better models to justify those valuations. More than $7 trillion will be spent scaling AI over the next five years, per Goldman Sachs. Frontier labs will have to generate a profit on that investment, which means outpacing competitors. That includes keeping customers from pivoting to open-weight model providers, which can be cheaper to run and are viewed by some as a safer alternative. Between the lines: AI is getting harder for anyone to monitor, making it unclear how the seemingly conflicted priorities of safety and rapid-fire model improvement can coexist. Daniel Kokotajlo, former OpenAI researcher and executive director of the AI Futures Project, said he doesn't believe AI can be safely scaled. Top AI companies should avoid putting the vast computing firepower at their disposal toward model improvement, a step that would force a slowdown, said Kokotajlo, whose team published the famed AI 2027 and 2040 essays . Researchers and AI employees involved in scaling "are doing something wrong," he said. Zoom in: Kokotajlo left OpenAI because of his own safety concerns in 2024. Since then, he's been invited to give talks to current employees about his research on AI safety. "The companies are just having this continuous process of conflicted feelings and internal discussion about like, what are we doing," he said. "Should we stop? Are we the good guys?" Reality check: Plenty of others, including President Trump, see a safe future for AI and point to the potential for liability — civil or criminal — if companies fail to make their products safe. "Whoever wins AI, WINS!" Trump wrote on Truth Social, reiterating that he won't be stifling or slowing down AI. "Human willpower is capable of figuring out how to safely scale these models," Akshay Krishnaswamy, chief architect at Palantir, told Axios, adding that one way to achieve this is through open models. The bottom line: As the industry is swept up in a riptide of AI slowdown rhetoric, it's unclear whether that's achievable in the near term.

06894867de8c.text: A distinctly Cold War calculus is looming over this week's Trump-Xi summit in Washington, as the U.S. and China weigh an emergency "red phone" for the day AI goes haywire. Why it matters: U.S.-China relations are so brittle that an AI hotline — not a trade pact, strategic slowdown or diplomatic reset — could emerge as the summit's most meaningful outcome. State of play: President Trump has spent the past week lashing out at AI "doomers" and boiling the race down to a single imperative: beat China. Trump has called AI-catastrophe fears a "HOAX" and vowed the U.S. would "not in any way hinder or stifle" AI as it fights to preserve its lead over Beijing. America's leading AI labs largely share Trump's urgency about China, but not his conclusion: many argue the intensity of the race is precisely why global safeguards are needed. The other side: China is every bit as determined to win the AI race, but its leader Xi Jinping — who lands in Washington Wednesday for his first state visit since 2015 — is balancing two competing fears: Falling behind: Xi has no interest in a safety regime that freezes the race with America still ahead. Beijing is pushing cheap, capable open-source models around the world while portraying U.S. chip controls and calls for restraint as a calculated effort to keep China down. Losing control: Xi wants AI powerful enough to transform China's economy, but never so powerful that it slips beyond the control of the Communist Party. Beijing focuses less on Silicon Valley-style extinction scenarios than on nearer-term dangers, like cyberattacks , malicious use and disruptions to critical infrastructure. Zoom in: That narrow overlap is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched Chinese officials this weekend on a "notification mechanism" for AI incidents with national-security implications. The Cold War precedent is the hotline Washington and Moscow established after the Cuban Missile Crisis — a direct channel designed to keep accidents and ambiguity from escalating into nuclear Armageddon. Trump and Xi are expected to discuss shared AI risks when they meet Thursday, while officials are also exploring a formal U.S.-China AI dialogue that could give the crisis channel a more permanent home. Reality check: So far, nobody has publicly defined what would make the red phone ring. In an AI catastrophe — say, a frontier model launches a major cyberattack on critical infrastructure — the first alarm may sound inside a private company rather than a military command center. That gets thorny fast: The lab may know more than the government about what its model is doing, while officials would have to decide how much sensitive information to share before they fully understand the threat themselves. Between the lines: Washington and Beijing already have crisis hotlines, as well as a history of going dark when they're needed most. China suspended military contacts after Nancy Pelosi's 2022 Taiwan visit . Months later, Beijing declined a Pentagon request for a call after the U.S. shot down its surveillance balloon — precisely the kind of tense, ambiguous moments the channels were built to defuse. COVID offered another warning: A cross-border threat that demanded transparency and cooperation instead fueled a bitter U.S.-China blame game over origins, information-sharing and responsibility. The bottom line: The very existence of the proposal is an acknowledgment that AI is no longer just another arena of U.S.-China competition. A serious failure on either side could quickly become a shared crisis.

Insurance Coverage Lags as Cancer Science, Treatment Move Forward
Eighteen months after his initial diagnosis, chemotherapy hadn’t slowed 21-year-old Mason Henderson’s rare brain tumor, which had spread to his spinal fluid. So he left his home in southeastern Texas to spend three weeks in a clinical trial in New York City.
But that failed, too, leaving a murky path for Henderson, whose cancer was so rare the World Health Organization had only given it a name in 2021. So early this year, Henderson’s doctors, evaluating his tumor’s deep genetic language, turned to a drug made by Merck and AstraZeneca called Lynparza.
It was not the standard of care for Henderson’s condition — there wasn’t really any standard, which is not unusual for rare cancers. And Henderson’s insurance would not pay for it, despite the careful justification given by the two specialists treating him.
“They have no guidelines for his cancer,” Henderson’s mother, Tabitha Lowe, said in a March interview with KFF Health News. “They’re discriminating against him because his cancer is so rare.”
Every year, tens of thousands of people — representing about a quarter of all U.S. cancers — are diagnosed with tumors that differ enough from frequently identified ones to be called rare. In determining whether to reimburse treatment for such ailments, insurers turn to Food and Drug Administration labels and expert guidelines.
But these rare afflictions often lack targeted, FDA-approved treatment options, even though in many cases, molecular tests offered by diagnostic companies and university labs can provide a strong suggestion of what will work.
“Insurance coverage routinely trails behind what genomic testing reveals about a patient’s cancer and what the science supports,” said Olivier Elemento, director of Weill Cornell Medicine’s Englander Institute for Precision Medicine.
Henderson’s neuro-oncologists, Jacob Mandel of the Baylor College of Medicine and Jessica Schulte of NYU Langone Health, decided to try Lynparza, also known by the generic name olaparib, in combination with chemotherapy. There wasn’t a wealth of evidence behind the drug but there was a “biologically reasonable” assumption it would help, Schulte said, because cells in tumors like Henderson’s have a flaw that drugs like Lynparza can target. Providers in several previous cases had seen brain cancers like Henderson’s respond well to the drug.
“In general, we try to base our treatment decisions on large patient studies” involving hundreds of patients, Schulte said. But large clinical trials will probably never be conducted for a cancer as rare as Henderson’s.
Schulte, who specializes in brain cancers in young adults, sees only a few of Henderson’s type each year, she said.
Mandel prescribed the drug on Jan. 16. Liviniti, Henderson’s pharmacy benefit manager, responded with a quick refusal on Jan. 30. Two weeks later, the company sent an explanation: “Lynparza is not approved for the diagnosis provided.” Out-of-pocket, the drug would cost about $8,700 per month, Lowe said. Liviniti did not respond to phone calls seeking comment.
Before his diagnosis, Henderson was a healthy, athletic young man with a big heart, faith in Jesus, and a tight group of friends, his mother said. At Evadale High School, north of Beaumont, Texas, Henderson played baseball and football and was homecoming king in 2022. After graduating, he worked at the local paper mill, spending his free time hunting, fishing, and exploring the woods on an all-terrain vehicle. He wanted to be a police officer, Lowe said.
Henderson was 20 on March 15, 2024, when his brother Gunner found him at the top of the stairs in the family home with his head in his hands. “He was in the post-seizure state,” Lowe said. “He couldn’t talk. Was crying. Trying to hug me. Could not communicate.”
At an emergency room in Beaumont, an MRI revealed a large tumor. He was transferred to Baylor St. Luke’s Medical Center in Houston and diagnosed with a form of brain cancer called diffuse hemispheric glioma (H3-G34 mutant).
Surgery a few days later cut out 90% of the tumor, but brain cancers are almost impossible to remove entirely, because of the delicacy of the tissue they’re embedded in, Schulte said.
After 16 months of radiation and chemotherapy, a September 2025 scan showed the cancer had spread to his spinal cord, a condition called leptomeningeal disease that usually proves fatal within a few months. Mandel contacted Schulte about a clinical trial she was leading. It consisted of 11 days of brutal craniospinal irradiation, which left Henderson exhausted. When it was over, the cancer was still there.
“The family was wonderful,” Schulte recalled. “They were trusting in their team, but they asked appropriate questions to make sure that we were thinking about Mason as a person.”
Coverage Refused
Lynparza, approved by the FDA in 2014 for ovarian cancer, works by interfering with tumor cells’ ability to multiply. After Liviniti, the pharmacy benefit manager, refused coverage for Henderson, his family turned to Jefferson County. Henderson’s stepfather, Jerry Lowe, flies helicopters for the county sheriff’s office.
The county, which had the final say on reimbursement because it pays claims directly for its employees’ family health coverage, also refused. When Henderson’s family appealed, the county review board authorized an independent medical reviewer to look at the case. The nonspecialist supported the board’s finding and recommended another drug, but Henderson’s doctors disagreed. The board didn’t respond to a request for comment.
AstraZeneca had also turned down the family’s request for a donation of the drug. By then it was March, six weeks after Lynparza was prescribed.
Cancers that start in the brain are unusual — only about 25,000 cases are diagnosed in the U.S. each year, compared with 320,000 breast cancers and 229,000 lung cancers. Only a few hundred people each year, mostly young adults, are diagnosed with Henderson’s type,

BOISE, Idaho — Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance.
When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600.
They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years.
“It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.”
The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured.
But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027.
The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments, especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry.
Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine, which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers.
“The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’”
As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans.
The number of people without insurance in the U.S. is expected to increase by roughly 15 million over 10 years because of the expiration of the expanded ACA subsidies and $1.1 trillion in estimated cuts resulting from President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
Healthier people are the most likely to opt out of insurance. That leaves insurance covering a smaller pool of people who tend to be sicker and need more expensive care. So insurers raise prices to cover the remaining enrollees, which fuels even higher premium costs.
‘Healthcare Is a Business’
Samantha LeGault, a nurse practitioner at a health clinic in Boise, said her employer-offered plan’s premium payment rose from $700 to $1,500 a month this year to insure herself, her husband, and four of their kids. LeGault has Crohn’s disease and two of their daughters also have medical conditions, so she said her family has no choice but to continue to pay for that health coverage.
But she decided to skip dental insurance to save money, and she prioritizes dental visits for her children over herself.
She had already struggled to set aside retirement savings and had switched her children from a private school they liked to public school to cut down on costs. Then the new health insurance costs tightened her budget even more. She estimated that about one-fifth of her income now goes toward her monthly premium payments.
“I know how the clinics work, that I am an expensive patient,” LeGault said. “At the end of the day, healthcare is a business in the United States.”
The Durhams have three other employees in their practice. Two of them receive health insurance through their spouses, Ashley Durham said. The Durhams said they pay $420 monthly toward their physician assistant’s premiums.
As a primary care physician, Joshua Durham said he doesn’t need regular doctor visits, because he can diagnose and treat himself — and, if needed, the rest of his family, though he acknowledged that’s frowned upon. The American Medical Association’s code of ethics generally discourages doctors from treating themselves or relatives but makes exceptions for emergency situations or short-term, minor problems. Ashley Durham said she’s filled prescriptions for her family.
Arthur Caplan, a bioethicist and professor emeritus at New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine, said that as more people are “turning toward relatives because they can’t access or easily see a regular doctor,” it may make sense to revisit that aspect of the code of ethics.
Out-of-Pocket Expenses
Healthcare workers with less advanced medical certifications than the Durhams often don’t have the option of treating themselves or family members — or don’t have savings to fall back on for healthcare expenses. And many healthcare professionals, such as Jill Kordick, a 64-year-old retired healthcare executive in Norwalk, Iowa, aren’t willing to go without the safety net of insurance.
In her work, Kordick saw hospitalizations become financially devastating for patients, so she said she would never opt out of health insurance — even for just the 16 months before she’d become eligible for Medicare at age 65.
Last year, she qualified for the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, allowing her to pay $75 a month for health coverage. Her premiums rose to $800 a month this year when those subsidies expired.
Because she has a $10,000 deductible, she put off going to the doctor for weeks when she had a sinus infection th

Almost nobody wants a data center for a neighbor. Residents fear noise and air pollution, excessive energy and water use and the loss of open land. In Pennsylvania, a hot spot for new data centers, researchers see an opportunity to solve some of these issues by taking advantage of a much older environmental hazard: abandoned coal mines.
Pennsylvania has the most abandoned coal mines in the country, totaling around 5,586 sites across the state. The state reports it would take roughly $5 billion to reclaim these polluted and sometimes dangerous areas, which have contaminated thousands of miles of waterways and are linked to underground fires, subsidence and sinkholes. At the same time, local opposition to data centers is growing.
Building data centers on abandoned mine lands would provide an alternative to destroying farmlands or local forests, instead making use of already unwanted acreage. Underground mine pools could cool data centers without relying on outside water sources. And companies could help shoulder cleanup costs of existing contamination. The idea is appealing enough that federal researchers investigated it in 2023, concluding that abandoned mine lands offer “land, power infrastructure, and mine water cooling” to data center developers, particularly in a place like Pennsylvania.
“If the data centers can demonstrate that they can clean up, treat the acid water and help restore their local environment, the local people are more likely to accept such development proposals,” says Zhongyang He, a researcher in Penn State’s Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering who’s been examining possible data center development on abandoned mine lands in the state. His research suggests that it’s a proposition worth pursuing—at least compared to building data centers in people’s non-polluted backyards. But could it actually work at scale? Or would Pennsylvania end up replacing one intractable environmental problem with another?
An Opportunity for Reuse
There’s already some proof of concept in western Pennsylvania, where a former mine has housed a data center since 2013. The site of an old limestone mine, Iron Mountain’s West Pennsylvania data center in Boyers sits 220 feet below ground, a 330,000-square-foot facility on a 315-acre campus that doesn’t bring in any outside water. Instead, the data center cools through a closed-loop system that relies on the 53-degree water in a 100-acre, underground lake (not a mine pool, but a comparable concept).
“We are using what the miners had left behind,” said Iron Mountain’s senior director of energy and sustainability, Chris Pennington. Boreholes, dug in mines to reach deep water or minerals, provide infrastructure for internet access, and data center clients appreciate the security of storing their information deep underground. Though the facility regularly recycles its lake water, Iron Mountain brings in some refrigeration to supplement the system.
Former coal mine sites in Western Pennsylvania slated to become data centers include the former Robena Mine in Greene County, which members of the county’s Planning Commission voted in favor of late last year and would use water from a nearby river that it would convert into steam. Another proposed data center at the former Consol coal mine in Washington County, owned by natural gas company CNX Resources, would use nearby natural gas reserves and “remediated mine gas,” per the Pittsburgh Business Times.
There’s precedent outside of Pennsylvania, too. In West Virginia, Energy DELTA Lab’s 450-acre Data Center Ridge boasts access to almost “10 billion gallons of underground water” for cooling at a former mine site. In Italy, an active dolomite mine is home to a data center located 328 feet underground, cooled by the surrounding rock and chilly air.
Typically in the 40s or low 50s degrees Fahrenheit, mine pool temperatures are theoretically low enough to cool data centers. Mechanical cooling accounts for around 40 percent of an average data center’s energy consumption, and medium-sized data centers can consume around 100 million gallons of water per year. Penn State researcher He and his colleagues found that of the 5,586 abandoned mine sites they analyzed in Pennsylvania, 160 had mine pools large enough to accommodate data centers (there are currently at least 100 data centers proposed in Pennsylvania).
He’s research team landed on other advantages in addition to natural cooling, like “legacy infrastructure,” he said. That could include proximity to roads and the electricity grid, which can be repurposed for data centers. Transmission lines powered large equipment at former mines, and some of that infrastructure remains. “That does not mean that…the line transmission capacity is enough for data centers,” He said, but it does mean relevant permits could be in place.
Both Penn State and the Eastern Pennsylvania Coalition for Abandoned Mine Reclamation have assessed a former mine in northeastern Pennsylvania called Morea as a possible data center site. It harbors an estimated 7 billion gallons of underground water via a nearby creek that was routed underground when the mine was active. It still has an electric transmission line, “sufficient for utility-scale solar or a large industrial facility, and expensive and slow to replicate,” per the coalition’s report.
That report also acknowledges the ongoing economic burdens carried by communities that once produced coal. In Mahanoy Township, home to the Morea site, the coalition notes a 20.3 percent poverty rate (compared to 11.6 percent statewide)—a commonality across former Pennsylvania mining regions. A study published in Nature in 2024 notes that people living in areas of Pennsylvania exposed to mine drainage had incomes 30 percent lower than people in unaffected areas.
Data center development could help with that. The federal report brings up the thousands of job opportunities that could materialize from abandoned coal mine restoration, which increase with da

On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpline to check if it was safe for her to travel.
She was excited about an advertising campaign she was going to shoot and showed her parents a photo of the cheque she had received as advance remuneration.
As she walked out of the door, she told her parents that she would be back in two days.
It was the last time the Salians saw their 28-year-old daughter alive.
On the intervening night of 8 and 9 June, Satish Salian was called by the police to a hospital where he learnt that his only child was dead.
Police said she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in the western city of Mumbai.
Disha's friends at the hospital said she had been drinking alcohol and fell accidentally.
Police later said their investigation had shown that her death was a suicide.
But earlier this month, the Bombay High Court ordered the federal police - the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) - to reopen the case and reinvestigate Disha's death.
The court order came after a petition filed last year by Satish Salian, who had insisted from the start that his daughter's death was not a suicide or an accident and alleged that she was gang-raped and murdered.
His allegations that some senior police officers had destroyed evidence and created a false story of suicide to protect some ministers and influential politicians who had a role in the alleged crime has made it one of India's most discussed deaths in recent years.
In the order, external on 2 September, Judges Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale criticised the police and said there were "too many glaring discrepancies" in their investigation, which was carried out in two phases over more than six years.
The judges insisted that they were not holding "a mini trial" but said "the investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers".
They pointed out the unexplained delay in police paperwork, that no blood had been found at the spot where the body had fallen and said that the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report did not seem consistent with a fall.
"We find this difficult to accept," they wrote.
One of the biggest criticisms from the court was that the police had only investigated it as a case of suspicious or unnatural death and not registered an FIR (First Information Report) - a document police have to prepare when they receive information about a crime.
Satish Salian's accusations are only allegations so far, but they have formed the basis of a new investigation by the CBI, which last week registered an FIR based on a written complaint from him.
The BBC has reviewed this FIR and read through the court order in the case.
Summarising Satish Salian's allegations, the court order said that at the time of her death, Disha was working with Kwan Entertainment - a celebrity management company - and represented Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput.
"She got to know about some objectionable activities of the powerful people. She gave that information to Rajput, who innocently divulged that to others. Ultimately that information reached back those people and she was murdered to silence her," it added.
Rajput mourned her death in an Instagram story. "It's such devastating news. My deepest condolences to Disha's family and friends. May your soul rest in peace," he wrote.
In the initial days, Disha's death went largely unnoticed until less than a week later, Rajput himself was found dead in his home.
Police also ruled his death to be a case of suicide, saying he had mental health issues for which he was under treatment.
But weeks later, his actress girlfriend Rhea Chakraborty was arrested following accusations from Rajput's father that she had contributed to his suicide. He also denied that his son had any mental health issues.
Following outrage, Sushant's case was also handed over to the CBI which, last year, closed the case, saying he had indeed died by suicide and that neither Chakraborty nor her family had a role in his death.
In the FIR Satish Salian has registered with the CBI, he has alleged that the deaths of Disha and Rajput are linked.
Disha, he says, shared with the actor "incriminating and objectionable information concerning alleged drug trafficking, child abuse and other unlawful activities" involving a former minister and some others and the two intended to hold a press conference to bring it into the public domain.
"In order to prevent that and protect the persons involved, a well-orchestrated criminal conspiracy was hatched. The victim was gang raped and murdered, and thereafter evidence was suppressed /fabricated and a false story of suicide was created to cover up the crimes and shield the accused."
In its order, the court said that registration of the FIR "does not imply any finding of guilt against anyone" and that no-one shall be treated as an accused unless the investigating officer finds "sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against them".
But as the FIR names some of the state's top politicians, police officers and Bollywood actors, the case has dominated headlines in India amid allegations of misuse of political power, denials and claims of political vendetta.
Satish Salian, who's been fighting for six years to get justice for his daughter, says he's felt "some peace" after the court ordered the fresh investigation into her death.
Disha, he told the BBC, was "very bright, she did well in her studies and read a lot. She had a heart of gold and was very helpful. She was our only child and she loved us very much".
His wife, he says, has been unable to come to terms with her tragic death and has gone into depression.
"I want the death penalty for those who hurt my daughter. Those who inflicted pain on her must die a painful death too. That is what justice for Disha would look like to me," he says.

A rare first edition of the novel To Kill A Mockingbird has been found among items donated to Oxfam, according to the charity.
The copy of Harper Lee's seminal 1960 work was discovered in a box of American books given to the charity's bookshop in Portobello Road, west London.
It has since been acquired by the British Library and will join its national collection.
Shop manager Olivia Haysman-Walker, who identified the copy as being a first US edition, said the book could easily have been missed. "There were lots of books to work through in the donation, but we recognised To Kill A Mockingbird and thought it was worth taking a closer look."
She added: "We realised quite quickly that we had something really special.
"The dust jacket showed its age, and although it was worn around the edges, the pages inside were in beautiful condition.
"It's amazing to think that this book has passed through our Oxfam bookshop and into the national collection at the British Library.
"It really has been quite a journey, and it's a lovely reminder, during Second Hand September, of the kind of treasures that can be hiding among the shelves and donations in our shops."
Second Hand September is Oxfam's annual campaign encouraging people to buy second-hand.
Lee's Pulitzer Prize-winning book tells the story of lawyer Atticus Finch as he defends Tom Robinson, a black man wrongly accused of raping a white woman.
Her story of racial injustice and childhood innocence, set in Alabama in 1934, has sold more than 40 million copies around the world and has been translated into 40 languages.
The US novelist, who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, died in 2016 at the age of 89.

The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different.
Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world?
The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's event was "bigger than London".
Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said.
A recent House of Commons report, external found that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022.
However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds.
"A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy.
"But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat.
"I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls.
"Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper."
Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be?
Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle.
She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House.
"London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old.
"You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do."
Bennett says you can harness the power of being different.
"Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says.
Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving.
"The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old.
Natalie Potter is network director at the British Fashion Council, and says the Fashion Britain initiative is "about recognising that British fashion is bigger than London".
Potter says that in the run up to LFW there were events in London, Bristol, Manchester, Liverpool, Newcastle, Edinburgh, Dundee and Cardiff.
But what happens after the catwalk leaves town?
Potter says the aim of Fashion Britain is that it will connect talent to "the infrastructure and opportunities that they need to grow".
"So working with the big global businesses that we do across the country to make sure that they've got routes to retail, to give them active mentorship," she explains.
Potter says this will happen "locally and regionally".
This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital.
"I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says.
"There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland".
Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week.
The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry.
"Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion.
"There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says.
For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world.
"Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic."

A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage.
The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave.
The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene.
Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects.
The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities.
The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them.
"The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action.
Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration.
Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible.
Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral.
The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police.
Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage.
Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl.
A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso.
Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention.
Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people.
Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added.
The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together.
Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers.
Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel, external the incident had brought "shame to society".
Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted.
She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible.
Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety.
Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices".
"This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter).
Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state.
Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action.
India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation.
The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy.
The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.

The News
US drone logistics company Zipline will expand a three-year pilot program to deliver health supplies to a third of the Ivorian population over the next eight years, the latest sign that African governments are increasingly comfortable with using drones to provide social services.
The deal will see Zipline build nine more facilities in CÃ´te dâIvoire to add to the sole operation it has run there since 2023. After using drones to deliver nearly 4 million medical products â mainly vaccines and blood â to more than 200 healthcare centers in a region northwest of Abidjan, Zipline has now locked in a long-term contract that could serve 12 million people, roughly a third of the Ivorian population.
The Ivorian government will pay Zipline for operating costs for eight years, especially for pharmacy-grade warehousing, cold chain, digital tracking, and delivery, Caitlin Burton, Ziplineâs head of global business said in a statement to Semafor. The company declined to say exactly how much it will receive, but expects the government to make a three-fold return on its investment.
The deal will ensure health facilities in areas that are difficult to access will receive âregular and secure supply,â Amadou Coulibaly, the Ivorian communications and digital economy minister, said earlier this month.
Know More
Zipline has operated drones in Africa for a decade and aims to be an on-demand delivery service. The Ivorian expansion builds on the companyâs first steps in Rwanda in 2016, and is part of an Africa-wide expansion play. In Nigeria, it plans to reach about half of the 220 million population by adding a dozen hubs to existing operations in three states.
Nearly $2 billion from venture capital investors has underpinned Ziplineâs global business that has grown from flying medical supplies to food delivery for Uber. It is in talks to raise $1 billion from Silicon Valley investors at nearly three times its most recent valuation of around $7.6 billion, according to reports last week.
But its Africa operations â which are still mostly about human health, with a gradual foray into livestock insemination â are benefitting from government funding. Zipline will cover its infrastructure costs in CÃ´te dâIvoire by unlocking money from a $150 million grant that the US government approved for the company last year. Washington conditioned the grant on Ziplineâs ability to secure expansion contracts from African governments and get them to cover operating costs.
Notable
- Nigerian drone maker Terra Industries this month secured two contracts worth $3 million from private companies to deploy its drones and other technology for surveillance over mineral sites, including one affiliated with the Africa Finance Corporation.

Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.
Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.
The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest attack in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.
All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the attack on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.
The accused had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms.

When Donald Trump unveiled a helipad at the White House on Monday, his remarks were barely audible in live footage of the event.
This was due to a row over an institution that rarely makes the news â the White House Press pool.
Yet it is at the heart of relations between the US president and the media, and this dispute could have constitutional implications.
Coverage of upcoming presidential engagements, which include the UN General Assembly in New York, could be affected.
What is the White House press pool?
It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday.
There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category.
The idea, conceived decades ago, is that having a pool saves on costs and space and it's not practical for hundreds of media outlets to follow the president around.
Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media.
The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation.
This latest row centres on the TV pool which has five members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC.
It began on Friday when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team.
A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled.
On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events.
That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad at the White House.
With no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks.
But there were no such problems at Trump's meeting later that day with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, because it was not dependent on pool cameras and lots of media were there.
Why did US networks pull out of filming Trump?
Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds the rotating role covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.
In a joint statement, the five networks said: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.
"No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."
The First Amendment of the US Constitution protects speech and press freedoms.
It forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Trump's speech to the United Nations on Tuesday will be unaffected by the boycott because it will be carried by outlets which are not part of the pool.
But the president's movements to and from his various New York events, which are usually filmed, could be subject to the blackout.
How has Trump reacted and what is Trump TV?
Responding to news of the lawsuit, Trump called the outlets "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements.
"Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He added that his team would file an appeal. Meanwhile the White House has launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube.
Its description reads: "Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place."
So far, the channel has primarily consisted of replays of previous Trump speeches and rallies.
For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York.
Unlike the traditional pool, however, that outlet is under no obligation to share material with others and has operated unilaterally for its audience.
Have there been previous examples of White House media bans?
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.
The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.
But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.

John Curtis (R-Utah) is urging Senate Judiciary leaders to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to investigate whether presidential family ties have been used for private family gain. Why it matters: The Republican Curtis is pressing a Republican-led Senate committee to scrutinize President Trump's eldest son, arguing the same congressional oversight applied to Hunter Biden should apply to presidential families of both parties. Driving the news: The Monday letter to Senate Judiciary chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) asks for an investigation into "private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access" tied to presidential family relationships. Curtis wants the committee to subpoena both sons to testify about "any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value." Catch up quick: ProPublica reported that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr.'s three-day wedding celebration in the Bahamas, including buying a private-island rental. Curtis also cited Trump Jr.'s ties to prediction markets. Trump Jr. is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket's advisory board. 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. is a partner, has invested in Polymarket. Curtis also pointed to Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving meetings with foreign heads of state, and Trump Jr.'s reported defense-sector investments. What he's saying: "A toaster is a wedding gift," Curtis wrote on X. "A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. 'Trust us' was not enough then, and it is not enough now." For the record: The White House, Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden have not yet responded to requests for comment. Hunter Biden has denied involving his father in business dealings. Trump Jr. confirmed Kremlev hosted celebrations, describing it as a wedding gift from a friend. President Trump later defended the arrangement as "totally allowed" and said he had been told his son would repay Kremlev. Flashback: House Republicans subpoenaed Hunter Biden in 2023 as part of their impeachment inquiry into then-President Biden. The younger Biden testified that he did not involve his father in his business dealings.
