The News
Saudi Arabiaâs auto manufacturing startup CEER unveiled its first cars, two luxury electric vehicles that will go on sale early next year as the kingdom doubles down on a bet that the industry can help drive its economic diversification.
The futuristic Exobot sedan and SUV have gull-wing doors and sweeping windscreens that stretch into the roof, a design that was personally picked by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Prices were not revealed, but CEER executives say the first models will target high-end buyers. Five more models at lower price points are planned by 2030.
The cars will be built at a new production plant on the kingdomâs west coast, north of Jeddah, capable of producing 240,000 vehicles. CEER was launched by the kingdomâs sovereign wealth fund in 2022 and its plant at King Abdullah Economic City is part of an emerging autos cluster that Saudi Arabia is developing in the hope of creating jobs, diversifying its economy, and boosting non-oil exports.
Production will begin in early 2027 and the first deliveries to customers are expected in March, chief executive Jim DeLuca told Semafor in an interview on the sidelines of the launch event.
âSaudi Arabia has wanted a car industry for a long time, there have been multiple attempts, and it has never come to fruition,â DeLuca said. âOur mission is to ignite that industry.â
Know More
CEER is part of a multibillion-dollar bet by Prince Mohammed to establish an auto industry after several failed attempts. Jaguar Land Rover abandoned plans for a Saudi manufacturing facility more than a decade ago and Toyota also walked away from talks in 2019.
The government has since shifted strategy. Public Investment Fund, which controls CEER in a partnership with Foxconn, invested in Lucid in 2018 and got the US EV maker to build the first auto plant in Saudi Arabia. That became an anchor for a wider cluster that includes Hyundai and suppliers such as Italyâs Pirelli, the USâs Lear, Koreaâs Shin Young, âGermanyâs Benteler, and Chinaâs Fangxin. Stellantis is also studying building a manufacturing facility in the kingdom.
CEER will initially be sold in the kingdom before expanding into other parts of the Gulf in 2028. It will face stiff competition as Chinese EV brands have been rapidly gaining market share in the region. CEERâs launch also comes at a time when many of Public Investment Fundâs other big projects have been facing budget cutbacks and a new focus on raising outside capital to help limit how much state funding they require. The fund aims to instill financial discipline and a more commercial mindset to boost returns.
DeLuca said CEER has not had any changes to its funding from PIF. âWe are fully funded,â he said, declining to comment on how much has been invested so far or when the company expects to become profitable. âThis plan to launch seven products between now and 2030 was developed and funded in 2023.â
The Exobot was supposed to go on sale in November, but supply chain disruptions from the Iran war caused a delay, he said, adding that no further impact from the war is expected.
PIF is also working on new deals to bring more suppliers into the autos cluster. That will help lift the local content in CEER cars from around 18% to 45% by 2034.
Matthewâs view
CEERâs first cars are definitely unique. The companyâs origin story is that the Saudi Crown Prince steered them into designing something unlike any other car. In that sense, they have delivered.
At Monday nightâs launch, several people compared the cars to a sci-fi movie. Car nerds in the audience broke out into applause as CEER unveiled 1,111 horsepower, a 670-km range, and zero to 100 km/h in 2.1 seconds for the top trims.
While that will undoubtedly make the models conversation starters, the key question will be whether that translates into sales. CEER executives are not giving away anything on the price yet, but given a combination of high-tech features and a complex design that may prove challenging to build in volume, it seems likely to come in at similar price levels to Lucidâs luxury EVs.
Lucid is a cautionary tale. The company has missed delivery targets, is losing more than $100,000 per car, and has required several new cash injections since PIF invested. More money will be needed.
CEER will have the advantage that being private keeps its finances out of public scrutiny. And as a strategic initiative for Prince Mohammed, CEER is likely to receive strong state support. But the management team will have their work cut out over the next few years to ensure that the kingdomâs sci-fi vehicles will hit the roads, at scale.

A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, who is in custody, confirmed his name and address from the dock at Westminster Magistrates' Court.
He was charged following a seven year British investigation into the killings.
He was told he faced a charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder, as a crime against humanity.
The case was passed to the Old Bailey for a hearing on 9 October. A bail application will be considered later on Tuesday.
The 1994 killings in Rwanda lasted 100 days, during which Hutu extremists carried out a campaign of slaughter against Tutsis and other moderate Hutus.
The charges against Brown relate to an alleged slaughter in the Rugenge district of Kigali between 6 April and 13 April in 1994.
Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as intending to destroy the group "as a whole or in part."
Prosecutors said he was being charged with genocide under the 2001 International Criminal Court Act and the alleged killings were "part of a widespread or systematic attack, directed against a civilian population, with knowledge of the attack."
Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son.
The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime.
Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.
In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda.
He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government.
Senior police officers have previously stressed the UK should not be a safe haven for alleged war criminals, and investigators have been trained in international war crimes legislation.
Sam Blom-Cooper, a barrister for Brown, told the court his client denied the allegations and was intent on going in front of a jury to clear the "stains of these appalling allegations."
He said the defendant had hoped for, longed for, and prayed for the best part of 20 years, for this day."
"These are appalling crimes, terrible murders committed in 1994 but this is the beginning of the end for Dr Brown."
Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda.

610028401a6d.text: Data: Zelle New Economics of Dating Report; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Rising costs are changing dating for more than eight in 10 Gen Z and millennial daters, leaving some to stop courting altogether, per new data from Zelle. The big picture: Young Americans are pushing off milestones under cost pressures — and the milestones themselves , from getting hitched to buying a home, are getting pricier once they get there. Driving the news: For younger Americans, just planning a date is a costly ordeal, with 17% of active Gen Z and Millennial daters saying they've gone into debt trying to maintain the dating lifestyle. Nearly one-third say they've gone on fewer dates amid rising costs. A smaller share, 11%, say they've stopped dating because they couldn't afford it. Members of Gen Z are more likely to split the cost of a date because of rising costs (26%) than Millennials (18%). Daters have changed strategies to lighten the cost burden — like suggesting free activities and spending more time on dates at home, which were used by 37% and 33% of active daters, respectively. The intrigue: As costs weigh on younger Americans, perhaps it's unsurprising that checkbook chemistry plays a big role in their love stories: Half of active daters say financial compatibility has at some point mattered more than romantic chemistry when deciding to keep dating someone. Men are more likely to say that than women (56% versus 45%), as are Gen Zers (53%) than Millennials (46%). But be warned: Talking money too much can kill the mood. For example, complaining about the price of everything or chatting too much about income would both give 47% of daters the "ick." What they're saying: "Dating has always come with unspoken rules, but rising costs are forcing a rewrite," Denise Leonhard, general manager of Zelle, said in a statement. "Financial compatibility is becoming part of the chemistry test. The new flex isn't running up the tab; it's reading the room, respecting the budget and showing thought." Zoom out: It comes as nearly all younger Americans (96%) reported being concerned about the cost of rent, groceries, gas or utilities, according to a recent Axios-Generation Lab poll of 18- to 34-year-olds. With the Game of Life ahead of them, high costs are leaving younger Americans struggling to even get on the board. Methodology: This online survey of 1,800 U.S. adults ages 18 and older was fielded August 14–25. Statistical testing is reported at the 95% confidence level. Go deeper: Youth poll: Thumbs down on everything

eb3cb2811962.text:
Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!
Alexis Nikole Nelson
Simon & Schuster, $35.00
I used to think that foraging for food would involve schlepping myself to a forest far from my urban home, a task that would demand an unpleasant car trip, practical shoes and insect repellent. But when I flipped through forager Alexis Nikole Nelson’s new book Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!, I discovered edible plants right in my neighborhood.
Linden trees, for example, are common across much of the United States, including in cities. They have edible leaves, flowers and fruits, Nelson explains. There’s one just down the block from the Science News office in Washington, D.C. And that is how I found myself, this summer, on tiptoe trying to reach as many green, pea-shaped fruits as I could hold.
And that’s not all. Dandelions, acorns, black walnuts, crab apples, roses, magnolias, serviceberries — all are edible treasures found within walking distance of my home. Nelson explains how to identify these and other plants and provides vegan recipes for dishes unlike anything found in grocery stores.
Awareness of local edible plants helps combat the “plant blindness” that pervades modern society. For many people, plants are a pleasant afterthought rather than a focal point of daily life. “Taking the time to get to know your plant neighbors helps even the most urban neighborhood … seem full of nature and whimsy, even if you have to look close to find it,” she writes.
The book’s cheeky title is a tagline Nelson uses in popular videos posted to her social media accounts, where she sometimes goes by “Black Forager.” (She uses humor to help viewers learn which plants are good for snacking and which ones might make you, uh, “unalive.”) Likewise, the joy Nelson injects into the book makes foraging approachable.
I was nervous about picking unfamiliar fruits from trees in public. Wouldn’t everyone think I was weird? But with Nelson’s encouragement I felt emboldened. While collecting my bounty of linden fruits, I had a few friendly conversations with passersby and had the opportunity to educate neighbors about the tree.
Linden is in the same family as cacao and it can serve as a chocolate substitute, Nelson explains. Following her recipe for linden ice cream, I roasted, ground and sifted my linden fruits. Then, I combined them with sugar, soy milk, vanilla and cornstarch and cooked and froze the mixture. The ice cream tasted like an earthier version of chocolate. Taste testers — some of my Science News colleagues — compared it to brownie batter, cereal milk and tea. But in fact, linden fruits are their own thing with their own incomparable flavor.
It was a fascinating project, but not a complete success. I collected just a fifth of the amount of fruit that Nelson suggested in her recipe, so I was able to make only about a cup of ice cream. And it had an unpleasantly grainy texture despite my best attempts at grinding and sifting.
But at least now I will never overlook a linden tree.
Buy Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! from Bookshop.org. Science News is a Bookshop.org affiliate and will earn a commission on purchases made from links in this article.

- Published
The developing El NiÃ±o climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures.
Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El NiÃ±o of 2015.
Some longer-term measures of El NiÃ±o have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.
El NiÃ±o can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt.
What is El NiÃ±o and how is it measured?
El NiÃ±o is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.
Forecasters track the development of El NiÃ±o by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El NiÃ±o is declared.
There are different ways of measuring the strength of El NiÃ±o, however.
The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average.
This is called the Oceanic NiÃ±o Index (ONI).
Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic NiÃ±o Index (RONI).
This measures how warm the key El NiÃ±o region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change.
By the RONI index the current El NiÃ±o is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks.
Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El NiÃ±o will be an unprecedented event.
"The fact that it has already exceeded previous records â with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year â shows the enormity of this El NiÃ±o."
Impacts of El NiÃ±o already being felt globally
Every El NiÃ±o is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed.
And the unprecedented strength of this El NiÃ±o does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather.
Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide."
El NiÃ±o increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others.
El NiÃ±o years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data.
Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal.
Another typical impact of El NiÃ±o is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere.
So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began.
Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia.
These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe.
Will there be an impact on UK weather?
The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El NiÃ±o tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions.
However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter.
A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.
The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El NiÃ±o, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.
In addition to storminess, El NiÃ±o can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El NiÃ±o.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El NiÃ±o winter and that was unseasonably warm.
As this unprecedented El NiÃ±o approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world.

- Published
A grand jury will not bring criminal charges against anyone in the death of a Mississippi teenager, who was found dead two days after a boating trip with friends on 4 July.
Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney hired by the family, had raised concerns that Nolan Wells, a black man, "ended up dead after going out on a boat with three young white men", and that there had been conflicting witness statements.
Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath said the grand jury indicated there was not enough evidence to charge someone with a crime in the death of Wells.
In a statement to US media, Crump said the grand jury result "leaves us with more questions than answers".
"Nolan's family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we," he said.
Police had said Wells accidentally drowned, with his friends saying he chose to stay back on Horn Island after they decided to leave early because of an issue with their boat.
A report from the grand jury posted on the district attorney's social media on Monday found that the "position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr Wells' body is consistent with drowning".
"There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan's death and disappearance were racially motivated," Myers McIlrath said in the video message.
According to the report, 25 grand jurors heard from 43 witnesses, including a forensic pathologist hired by Wells' family to conduct an independent autopsy.
"The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 ... engaged in any criminal conduct related to âthe death of Mr. Wells," the report said.
The report said those who travelled with Wells were fully cooperative and offered GPS devices, surveillance footage, cell phones and other evidence.
It also said it is not unusual for visitors to Horn Island to stay and leave on different boats than they came on on crowded holiday days.
Wells' mother Christine Wonsley was the first to raise the alarm that her son, who played American football at Southwest Mississippi Community College and was described by his coach as a "happy-go-lucky kid", had gone missing after he did not return on the evening of 4 July.
Authorities discovered his body off the coast of the island on 6 July, following a search that included multiple local, state and federal agencies.

- Published
An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.
That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.
But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.
And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.
No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.
So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?
Venue changes have not quietened protests
As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza.
In May a friendly match the Republic of Ireland played against Qatar in Dublin was twice interrupted after fans threw tennis balls onto the pitch featuring the Palestinian flag.
The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott.
Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income.
As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures.
No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary.
Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.
The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".
Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.
The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.
In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.
The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.
Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.
FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".
"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".
The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".
Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing
The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).
In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice.
The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers.
On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population."
Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

The world must build more than 6 terawatts of renewable power in the next five years â more than all previous years combined â to deliver on a goal to triple global renewable energy capacity by 2030, according to a new report. At COP28 in the UAE in 2023, countries agreed to collectively reach 11.2 TW of installed renewable capacity by 2030. Last year, clean power representing a record 693 GW of new capacity was added, but that pales in comparison to the 1,200 GW needed on average every year to 2030 to meet the goal, according to the report by the International Renewable Energy Agency, the Global Renewables Alliance and the COP31 Presidency.
Delivering the extra capacity requires an additional $8.6 trillion in investment over 2026-2030, the report found. To enable the additional renewable capacity to come online, investment to expand, modernize, and build flexibility on the grid must average up to $1 trillion a year, up from $525 billion in 2025.

The defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case.
The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out.
A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing".
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this.
Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home.
Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time.
Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children.
In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated.
He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires.
In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her.
Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him.
The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial.
"If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote.
Several jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

5acf4e28be07.text: By — Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-live-trump-addresses-2026-united-nations-general-assembly Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump addresses 2026 United Nations General Assembly World Sep 22, 2026 9:26 AM EDT WATCH LIVE: Day 1 of the 2026 United Nations General Assembly NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is set to address the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday at a tumultuous moment for the world — and for his presidency. President Donald Trump will address the U.S. General Assembly on Tuesday. Watch live in our video player above. The global economy has been shaken by his decision to launch a war against Iran. Anxiety about the social impact being wrought by artificial intelligence is surging. And questions linger about the future of the United Nations itself with Trump's scaling back U.S. financial support for the United Nations. WATCH: Press pool declines to cover Trump in protest of his ban on news outlets After his speech to the annual gathering of world leaders, Trump is expected to hold talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and a more informal meeting with Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez, according to the White House. He's also set to meet with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council nations — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates — to discuss the way ahead with the war in Iran and growing concern about recent Iran-backed rebel attacks on Saudi Arabia. The visit to the U.N. comes when Trump's foreign policy approach — particularly his decision to start a war with Iran — has become a drag on his fellow Republicans' hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections. Nevertheless, administration officials signaled Trump will make the case in his address that the world is better off for his leadership. READ MORE: Britain's Burnham to meet Trump and make UN debut after offering UK military support for Saudis "We expect the president will highlight how he has and his administration have confronted complex problems head-on around the world," Ambassador Mike Waltz, Trump's chief envoy to the international body, told reporters. Waltz also suggested that Trump might revisit some of his long-held criticism of the United Nations. The president has criticized the body as being ineffectual on issues of war and peace, has claimed the organization is perpetuating a "con job" by emphasizing the need to address global warming, and has asserted the U.N. has promoted the "invasion" of migrants into Europe. Iran war to loom large In last year's address at the U.N., Trump claimed the U.S. had "demolished" Iran's nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities. He returns to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran. The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the United States and Israel have killed much of Iran's top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles. READ MORE: Why Trump is rolling out the red carpet for Xi after years of slamming China The passage of oil from other Gulf countries through the Strait of Hormuz has improved in recent weeks with the help of the U.S. Navy helping guide commercial vessels through the narrow waterway. Still, the flow of oil is significantly below pre-war levels. And Brent crude continues to hover around $100 per barrel, up from about the $70 range in the weeks before the start of the war. The energy market continues to be spooked. Saudi Arabia earlier this month shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf. The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq. At the same time, territorial grabs by the Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iranian-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait has now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane. Majed al-Ansari, chief spokesman for the Qatari Foreign Ministry, said Monday that Qatar and other mediators are trying to penetrate a "deep deficit of trust" between the U.S. and Iran and get the sides back to negotiations. "Either we sign a deal now or sign a deal 10 months away," said said al-Ansari, speaking at the Concordia Annual Summit, a global affairs forum taking place during the U.N.'s high-level week. The only difference is the number of dead and destruction that we see." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Trump is open to meeting with Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, while he's in New York for the General Assembly. "This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you're going to solve problems," Rubio said on NBC's "Today" show. "It doesn't mean you're going to end up agreeing with them, but it's important." The administration will sign a Greenland deal At last year's General Assembly, Trump touted his record as a peacemaker and claimed that "everyone says that I should get the Nobel Peace Prize" for his administration's efforts mediating several conflicts around the globe. This year, his administration is set to sign an agreement on the sidelines of the General Assembly with Danish and Greenlandic leaders that aims to set the pathway for the expansion of the U.S. military's footprint on Greenland. The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to "take over" Greenland, a territory of NATO-ally Denmark, by military force if necessary. Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark's territory. Trump's frustration with Russia-Ukraine war mount

A British man has pleaded guilty to causing the death of his two-year-old son who fell from a hotel window in Cyprus.
The father, from Essex, admitted a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act at a court in Paphos on Tuesday.
The boy fell from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the Times had previously reported.
A further hearing will take place on 5 October when the prosecutor will set out the facts of the case and the defence will present mitigation, a court official confirmed.
The defendant's name was not given during the hearing.
The man was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week in order for the plea hearing to take place.
His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing.
Paphos district court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side.
The father decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said.
A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing.
"The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said.
The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence.
